speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: While hon. members on both sides have worked together, I think very effectively, to improve this measure from the form in which it was originally introduced, I feel it is unfortunate that it is necessary to conclude our efforts by those on this side being obliged to take very strong exception to the change made by the government in the method of the appointment of returning officers. It is not in this bill, but the franchise commissioner is appointed under this bill and the power which was formerly exercised by the chief electoral officer is hereafter to be exercised by the governor in council. I for one had the impression, when the franchise measure was introduced, that it was understood there would be a new officer in the person of the franchise commissioner and that while he would have the appointing of revising officers, the chief electoral officer would remain in control of the electoral machinery and that the appointment of returning officers would continue to be under his direction: in other words, that there would foe something of equality as between these two officers representing in a way the shades of opinion, speaking again very broadly, which are generally prevalent in the country. I do not know why the government has changed from what I believe was its original intention in that regard. Certainly I for one had that impression

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not after the first
meeting.

I had very strongly the impression that the chief electoral officer would continue, and I believe it was not until the Minister of Justice himself at a later stage told us in this house of the changes that were to be made in the general election act that any of us had the idea that the appointment of returning officers was to be brought again under the governor in council.	-

Dominion Franchise Act
For many years past there has been a difference of view between the hon. gentlemen opposite and ourselves as to the appointment of election officials. We have held that election officials should as far as possible be non partisan and chosen where possible from persons holding particular positions rather than that their appointment should be made on a party patronage basis; and certainly, so far as the Liberal party when in office is concerned, we have proceeded along the line of endeavouring to secure in the appointment of returning officers persons already holding public offices, whereever that was possible, and so far as was possible officials who would be acceptable to members on both sides of the house. I think a most unfortunate departure is being made at the present time.
Under the British North America Act, 1867, section 42, appointment of returning officers was in the discretion of the governor general, which meant of course the governor in council.
Under the first Dominion Elections Act, 1874 (37 Viet. chap. 9) discretion was taken away from the governor general and the writ issued to the sheriff or registrar of deeds for the electoral district. The governor general had power to choose only in districts where there were no such officers. This was, and still is, the position in Great Britain.
In 1892, the governor general was given discretion in the matter of the appointment of deputy returning officers, and that continued until 1925; but in 1925 the law was amended to provide that returning officers, instead of being appointed for the particular election, should hold office during pleasure like other servants of the crown. That certainly is a position which it seems to me this parliament ought to seek to maintain-to secure in returning officers those who will feel that their continuance in office is not dependent on the particular administration in power, but rather that they are like other public servants, holding office during pleasure and, presumably, indefinitely, on the condition of good behaviour and the satisfactory discharge of their duties.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They only work six weeks in four years,

Yes, but the
principle remains the same, whether it be six days or six years or sixty. It is a question either of trying to maintain a civil service independent of patronage or of resorting to the patronage method in as many directions as possible. While in 1925 the Liberal administration of that day adopted the practice I have just mentioned, the shadow govern-

ment of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, a year later took office. Though holding office only for a few weeks in that time they changed that arrangement, and under the Meighen government most of the appointments of returning officers made in 1925 were cancelled and new officers were appointed. When the Liberal administration came back into power and before the general election of 1930 the discretion and the power of recommendation was taken out of the hands of political parties and appointments were placed entirely under the jurisdiction of the chief electoral officer. That was evidence of a desire to secure strict impartiality as between all parties in the choice of returning officers, and I think the chief electoral officer did endeavour in making his appointments to see that those who were appointed would be persona grata to members on all sides of the house. The amendments this year take this discretion away from the chief electoral officer and restore it to political partisans. That is a very serious departure from what was an exceptionally good rule to follow. I have in my hand a statement which serves to illustrate the nonpartisan character of the appointees under the late Liberal administration. I will not read it now but it may be given later. What I rise for at the moment, before the bill passes, is to protest as strongly as I can against this return to patronage in the appointment of returning officers. It is conclusive evidence that the government is seeking to get the whole of the electoral machinery into its own hands and under the control of its own partisan appointees, in a manner which cannot fail to occasion lack of confidence in the method of administering the electoral act.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Last night I took strong
exception to the passing of the clause which disqualifies among others a sect of the Douk-hobors resident in British Columbia and also the descendants of any such Doukhobors. I do not think it is necessary for me to repeat what I said then. I feel it is an exceedingly dangerous proceeding. The Doukhobors are not a race but a religious sect. It is dangerous to disqualify certain people because they belong to a particular religious sect. It may be extremely difficult to ascertain just who are Doukhobors because they cannot be judged by their nationality. Further than that, this section seeks to make the descendants of certain religious believers follow of necessity the religion of their fathers, and to disqualify them whether or not they wish to follow that religion. It seems to me an exceedingly dangerous pro-
JUNE 30, 1934	ST 1	4529
Dominion Franchise Act
posal, and without covering the ground again, in order that the matter may be placed before the house for decision, I would move that the bill be not now read the third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they have power to amend section 4 by striking out (xii) of subsection (1). That motion is seconded by Mr. Jacobs.

I presume that one can discuss this amendment for a moment or two. I approve of it. I think it will be a standing disgrace to this none too graceful session, so far as legislation is concerned, if this amendment is not accepted. There is one significant matter that I wish to call attention to, without going over the ground I covered last evening. I am not going over the ground that I went over last evening. But, Mr. Speaker, did you notice the two hon. members on the other side who got up to defend this outrage and to defend the government? The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) and the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) were, according to my recollection, the only two hon. gentlemen to defend the government's disfranchisement of the Doukhobors. Was there any particular reason for these two hon. gentlemen defending this legislation? Are their seats, as good Conservative ones, in danger? Is this the location of these Doukhobor settlements-in Yale and West Kootenay? If it is, then it would have been very much better for them if somebody other than they had stepped forward and tried at least to defend the government's outrageous legislation in this respect. I feel so strongly on this question I scarcely dare trust myself to talk about it at all. To think in Canada in this day of grace, when we are trying to develop a better civilization, anybody or any government would dare to do such a thing is past my comprehension.
I did not mention all the minorities to whom this legislation might be applied. We have our Mennonite brethren also holding peculiar religious tenets; my deskmate (Mr. Euler), I understand, is a third generation Mennonite. Is the government going to follow these third generation Doukhobors to heaven and gone, I will put if in that way, and disfranchise them all the way ? How many crosses will it take to get the Doukhobor blood out of them and thereby qualify them for citizenship? If peculiar people are going to be disfranchised, how many of us will be left with the franchise? The world is full of extraordinary religious sects. I have heard of
people in a very prominent religious denomination who actually would not worship with other denominations such as the Methodists and Congregationalists. Is the government going to disfranchise them too? It will come pretty close home to the Minister of Justice, if they do. So, I say, beware of establishing a precedent of this nature that because people entertain strange religious views, this entitles them to disfranchisement and they are not to be called citizens of Canada. That is all I have to say; I am merely warning the government, when they make a precedent of this nature, how very far-reaching it is and no man knows for instance, upon whose head the disfranchising axe may next fall.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say half a dozen words on this subject. This has nothing to do with religion in any way, shape or form; it has nothing to do with the religious beliefs of the people in question in any way, shape or form.
With what has it to do, then?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It has to do with the fact that these people have openly and successfully, mark you! defied Canada and the laws of Canada. They simply said: We will not be enumerated as citizens of Canada and they have succeeded, I am sorry to say, in preventing their names from being recorded as citizens. If they are unwilling to be recorded as citizens they are not going to vote as citizens. That is all there is about the matter.
Let us look at the situation. In every statute that has ever been passed in this country dealing with the franchise, there have been disfranchisements. It must be within the memory of most hon. members that in Nova Scotia while the late Mr. Fielding was premier of that province, no dominion civil servant could vote; every dominion civil servant was disfranchised in that province.

If that was the law
then, this shows no advance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That was the law. In all our statutes concerning dominion elections there are disfranchisements of certain named individuals. In the province of Quebec women cannot vote; they are disfranchised; every woman is disfranchised in the provincial elections in Quebec. Is that a blot upon the civilization of that province? Quebec has said: We do not want our women to vote.
Dominion Franchise Act

They have a perfect right to say that and, what is more, the people have approved that action on more than one occasion.
We do not observe that in our dominion franchise with regard to the women of Quebec.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Exactly; that is what I say, but in Quebec they do not permit the women to vote in provincial elections. I am only answering the argument that this is an effort to disbar a person for a particular reason that has to do with religion and to point out that ever since the franchise was established in Canada there have been exceptions to the general rule that all persons vote. It would take too long to deal with the history of the establishment of the franchise down to the days of universal franchise, but it is sufficient for my purpose to say that the Doubhobors are not disfranchised because of religion or politics; they are disfranchised because they have successfully defied the law of Canada to enumerate them as citizens of Canada, and I repeat: If they are not willing to become citizens of Canada and openly defy the law, then they should not be permitted to vote as citizens.

In view of
what the Prime Minister has just said, may I ask him this question: Would not a better way to proceed have been to enact in the Franchise Act that any person who defies the law to the extent of refusing to be enumerated as a Canadian citizen shall not 'be qualified to vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That cannot be done.
Then innocent parties should not be discriminated against, or as Burke says, you cannot indict a nation; no more can you indict an entire race or all members of any religious sect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I say that it is impossible to work that out, as the right hon. gentleman will see in a minute, because there is no general defiance of the law except by those particular people in the one province of British Columbia. They have simply said: We will not be enumerated and they drove off with pitchforks, arms and missiles the people who tried to enumerate them and succeeded in preventing their being enumerated except by force.
Perhaps some of them were willing to be enumerated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They were not; they
were given a chance.

Did they refuse to be
enumerated?

speechtext:

opportunity, and refused.

I wonder whether
the Prime Minister is aware that some of the Doukhobors themselves assisted in the taking of the last census?

speechtext:

know an effort was made-does the hon. member mean in Saskatchewan?

No, in British
Columbia.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I know in British Columbia as a last resort we endeavoured to ascertain whether we could secure the aid of some of them in taking the census, and we failed.

secured.

Mr. Speaker, I am willing to admit
that this matter has nothing to do with religion but I am very much afraid it has something to do with political considerations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What nonsense!

I want
to repeat what I said last night; I am in favour of applying the utmost rigor of the law against any lawbreaker in any part of the dominion, but I tell the Prime Minister and the two hon. members who spoke to defend the government's action-
Three hon. members.

-that it is the wrong method to punish any person in Canada by depriving him of his vote. The province of British Columbia has punished these men and properly so but it is a pernicious, vicious and iniquitous principle to single out any race by name in any legislation of this country and to deprive them of the franchise because this will affect not only the people there to-day but their descendants to the third and fourth generation. The Prime Minister of Canada by this legislation is visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children who in years to come may be the very finest of our Canadian citizens. This condition is not to be permanent; I trust these people with education and experience in the dominion will do what other races have done and grow up to be the very best of Canadian citizens. But here we are to-day as a parliament representing all free peoples within this country, saying that any man because he is a Doukhobor is absolutely

Dominion Franchise Act
deprived of the franchise and his sons and daughters and their descendants unto untold generations are also to be disfranchised. That is the most Tory measure I ever heard of in any parliament.

I wish to state my position, I

This House of Commons could not exist if defiance of law were permitted. This house exists because of the cooperation of the people in the enforcement of the laws. That is the genius of democracy, the cooperation of the people with the government. I am not convinced that this policy is not sound.

Very briefly, and really on one point only I wish to speak, because I have no defence to make of people who violate the law. But I think it is a dangerous principle to disfranchise any group of people
By name.

By name or by race or because of the religious beliefs they may hold. But I want to point out for the cool consideration of the government, what possible justice can there be in disfranchising the descendants of these people, who cannot possibly be held responsible for the sins, if you call them that, of their parents? It is utterly unjust and unfair and I see nothing in defence of it. I am referring particularly to that provision which says that the descendants of the Doukhobors shall be disfranchised. Probably there will be children of Doukhobors now living who will marry into some other sect, become converts to another faith, refusing to follow their parents in sentiment or religion.

The Prime Minister said that they are not disfranchised because of their race-

Hear,

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to register my protest against this legislation.
Air. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. Last year, when I addressed you as Air. Chairman, an hon. gentleman said that I should address you as Mr. Speaker. I now rise to the same point of order.

With all due respect, Mr. Speaker, to our hon. friend from Temiscouata (Air. Pouliot) I just wish to register my protest against this piece of legislation. The majority of the citizens of this country are in favour of being good to the humble, to the weak and to minorities, whatever may be the opinion of the right hon. Prime Minister about qualifying minorities or others. It is a principle of our criminal law that it is better to free ninety-nine guilty men than to condemn an innocent one. In this legislation they put in one bag all the citizens who belong to a nationality or race and say that because they belong to such a race they are to be deprived of their right of citizenship-
They are not a race.

-and of the privileges
attached to it. I say this is absolutely wrong, and following that principle of our criminal law, even if there is only one Doukhobor who abides by the laws of the country he should be granted the right to vote. I am sure, like those members who are conversant with these people, that hundreds and thousands of them abide by the law of this country. To govern the citizens of Canada we have criminal, civil and common law. If any citizen, whatever his race, his religion or his allegiance, does not abide by the laws of this country he may be brought into court and, if convicted, sentenced to fine or imprisonment. We have been told that the Doukhobors refuse to abide by the laws of Canada. Let us condemn those who refuse to do so but let us not interfere with those who do abide by our laws.
I am very much in favour of amending this provision because I belong to one of the races that is in the minority in this country. It may happen that I will not come back to this

house-which I should regret-due to the fact that I have been deprived of my riding. That has not been done because the county of Laprairie-Napierville is one which should not be represented in this house; that is so because the Prime Minister of this country said, "We are not going to be governed by an arrogant minority." So I feel very keenly the fact that in this legislation the government deal with a whole race whom they have allowed to become citizens of this country. For the sake of argument let us say that the majority of them refuse to abide by our laws, but now the government are going to refuse to allow the remainder to vote and take advantage of the other privileges to which they are entitled as British subjects. If these people refuse to become British subjects let them be deported; so long as they remain here as British subjects they should have all the privileges and rights as well as all the responsibilities of British subjects.

A higher authority than I ever hope to be has declared that there is a time to talk and a time to keep silence. Inasmuch as we are about to prorogue at any moment I think I will follow that advice and say what I have to say in a very few words, particularly as I had something to say on this question when it was up last night.
The Prime Minister makes the statement that these Doukhobors should be disfranchised because certain outrages were committed by some of their race in British Columbia. I do not know that we have a clear definition of what a Doukhobor is. I do not know; there is no interpretation of the word in the bill. How is a judge to decide who a Doukhobor is unless he comes into court without clothes? I cannot understand how the Prime Minister, who is a profound lawyer and a man of the world, could agree to a section of this kind becoming part of the law of our country; that is what surprises me. I have always had a very high admiration for the talents of the right hon. gentleman, but this time he has fallen in my estimation. I can only suppose that we have had so much heavy work during the last five or six months that he is slipping a bit, and if legislation of this kind is going to be introduced I think it is high time we closed parliament for this session.
I suppose the race to which I belong has suffered more from legislation of this sort than any other race. This is the introduction of Hitlerism into the parliament of Canada. In Germany, under the laws of the third Reich, it is declared that any person found to have Jewish blood in his veins as far back as the
year 1800 is deprived of his status as a citizen In what respect does that provision differ from this law, except that we are visiting the sins of the father upon the children to the third and fourth generation while they are visiting the sins of the children on the fathers? As between the two I should- say they were the most logical, because we know the history of the fathers while we cannot know the history of the children. I am surprised that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister should say that every Doukhobor now residing in British Columbia, and his descendants to the last generation, should be deprived of the right to vote because of certain incendiarism and other offences which have been committed in British Columbia. Surely that is not the well considered view of the Prime Minister of this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Neither is it the view he puts forward.

It resolves itself into this section of the law; that is what it means. It seems that in British Columbia disfranchising people is a favourite sport, because the Doukhobors are not the only people disfranchised there. There are the Japanese, the Chinese and so on, but I do not intend to raise that question. I remember that some ten or twelve years ago I offered some criticism of the system in British Columbia with regard to the disfranchising of citizens, and I walked into a hornet's nest prepared by my good friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I still remember the castigation I received at his hands, or rather at his tongue, at that time. So I am not going into that question, but I say this thing is spreading. To-day we have it to a certain extent in the province of Quebec; only last winter a follower of the Prime Minister, sitting on the government side, made a remarkable statement. I was not in the house at the time, and the two members of my persuasion who were in the house did not understand French. This is what the hon. gentleman said, according to Hansard of February 26 of last year:
I would suggest to them-
He was speaking to the opposition:
-if they are so anxious to work in the interests of their race, to travel down in groups to Quebec so as to request the government of that province to see that the chairmen of the two most important committees of the legislative assembly be French Canadians instead of being Jews, in the only Catholic province of Canada, as the Hon. Mr. Taschereau delights to call it.
There we have Hitlerism exposed in all its hideousness, in the province of Quebec, and now we find this new law coming into force
Dominion Franchise Act

which will only encourage men of the type of the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) to continue that sort of work. I say a statement of that kind is not becoming to a member of the House of Commons, no matter on what side of the house he sits. It was offensive to me, Mr. Speaker, to see that gentleman invited time and again to act as chairman of the committees of the house in which I had to sit, and to have to address my remarks to him. I say he does not deserve to be in the parliament of Canada. This was the first time any statement of that kind was ever made in this house. Of course he received his just deserts from the premier of Quebec and from others who gave expression to their opinions in the public press. I have not heard any hon. member opposite rise from his seat and protest against that kind of conduct. If we are going to allow legislation of this kind to pass to-day, tomorrow we will have the hon. member for Compton or others of the same frame of mind declaring that in the province of Quebec the Jews should not be permitted to appeal to the electorate for election to parliament. This is how it could be done: Supposing in a moment of madness a man like the hon. member for Compton might have the reins of power-Lord forbid-in the province of Quebec. He would pass a franchise act declaring that no Jew could sit in the legislature of the province of Quebec or the parliament of Canada. He would ask that the law of the province of Quebec should be carried into the dominion franchise act. In such an event where would I be? Where would my colleagues be? Where would the Jewish people, even unto the fourth, fifth, or sixth generations be? They would be in the same position as the Doukhobors.
But you would still have your clothes on.

Yes, I would have my
clothes on, but I would not be permitted to show them. You would not see me here. That is the sort of thing that happens when we tamper with the franchise, and when we declare who should and should not be allowed to do this or that. The majority can declare whatever they like. It is always the majority that declares the minority is unfit to do this or to do that. AVe had a statement made yesterday by the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) to the effect that this had all been arranged beforehand. He said the Doukhobors had agreed that if they were given exemption from military service they would not ask for the vote, and the franchise would be taken from them. He said they
[Mr. Jacobs.!
were happy about it. They sold their birthright for a mess of pottage; they did not know what they were doing. They were sacrificing their rights as citizens of this country to obtain exemption from military service which service, I understand, is contrary to their religious views. So I think those of us who are fair minded and who look at things from a wider viewpoint than the go'vernment, see that we are quite within our rights in making a protest.
May I point out to the Prime Minister that the great dominion of Australia was at one time a penal colony, and everyone sent there was sent as a convict. Their descendants, the second, third and fourth generations are now at the head of the government. They went out in the first instance in the government's service, and they have remained in the government service-although in different degrees. I think the Australians would be offended if they knew that W'e treat our people in the way indicated to-day. They took their convicts, and developed them into first class citizens-sons of the morning, children of the light, and so on. They consider themselves in every respect the same as we are, and they are quite right. I do not for one moment wish to compare, for instance, Mr. Stanley Bruce who was entertained in Ottawa only a short time ago, with the poor Doukhobors who, without knowledge of the law, offend. Alter all, is it not part of our theory that we are carrying the white man's burden. We are looking after the "silent, sullen people," as Kipling says, half devil and half child-because that is all the Doukhobors are. It is part of the white man's burden to educate them to our standards. Certainly we are not going to achieve that end by disfranchising them and treating them as pariahs. I do not believe that to be the Christian idea of the condition which should prevail-and may I add, in passing, that I do not hold myself out as a teacher of Christianity. But I am in favour of a Christianity which Christianizes people, and it certainly comes with very poor grace from me, the only non-Christian in this house to-day, to tell Christian people what Christianity should be. Particularly is that so in regard to the Prime Minister, a man who has always represented the very best type of Christianity, a man whom I have admired for many years because of his talents, his wide and broad views respecting the Jewish people and the persecutions they have suffered, notwithstanding the views of some of his camp followers who sit behind him'. What surprises me is that the Prime

May I, at the outset, state that I am absolutely in agreement with this measure. Hon. members opposite state that we are disfranchising not only those living to-day but their children and grandchildren. We are not passing legislation today which could not be changed at the prdper time. For that reason I think the arguments advanced by hon. members opposite to the effect that we are disfranchising not only present day Doukhobors, but Doukhobors of the future, are absolutely silly-and I do not use the term offensively.
I now come to the reference made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. Had he wished to quote at greater length from my remarks he would have disclosed that the views he obtained were only incidental to the remarks I made. When I made the remarks to which the hon. member has referred I was referring to hon. members opposite who on the occasion in question were trying, as they have had the habit of doing, to place themselves before the people of the province of Quebec as the great champions of their race, their religion and their rights. I was simply stating that if they were so anxious to render service to their race and their creed, there were many other fields of activity which were more important, so far as race and creed were concerned, than the question under discussion at that time. That reference was only incidental, and I do not consider that I attacked the Jewish people in any way. the gold standard in more ways than one perhaps a few remarks on this vicious bill will be in order. When examining the Doukbobor provisions of this bill one comes to the conclusion that between the policies of the Conservative and the Liberal parties a great gulf exists-the gulf of civil and religious liberty and of fairness and justice to mankind. I should like to range myself with those on this side who stand for freedom whenever that question presents itself. I do not need to say that I belong to a race that has fought valiantly for its freedom; I belong to a race that has never been conquered and never will be conquered while it remains true to the principles of freedom and liberty. I would be ashamed of my race if those who represent it in this house did not stand up on an occasion of this kind to fight for those from whom the right of the franchise is being taken.
Certain outrages have been charged to our Doukhobor friends. I do not think there is an bon. member in the house who is so closely related to one of those outrages as myself. I had a first cousin in the coach in which Verigin was blown to pieces. Some of my direct relatives blamed the Doukhobors for that outrage, but I do not. I investigated the matter and I found out from Canadian National Railways men that that outrage was never committed by the Doukhobors, it was committed 'by the Canadian National Railways authorities carrying loose dynamite from one point to another on the railway. This is a case where the Doukhobors were blamed for an outrage for which they were not guilty. They are blamed for many other things for which they are not guilty. The very reason for this bill is based on such unproven outrages and political fear and to have such a foundation for a bill of this kind is not conducive to good and progressive citizenship. Therefore, I am opposed to it.
I have a few Doukhobors in my riding. I doubt if there is another riding in Canada which is as cosmopolitan as the riding of North Battleford. We have some Doukhobors there, Belgians, French from the old land, Germans, Ukrainians, British, Americans and Norwegians.
No Scotch!

Yes, they are everywhere, God bless them. I must say that our Doukhobor settlers have lived up to the law and have proved to be respectable and industrious citizens ever since they came to Saskatchewan. They have prospered on their farms and have brought wild areas into cultivation. They
r.Mr. McIntosh.]
have built splendid homes and have made money. They have not been on relief like many of the British people have been for the last three or four years. My hon. friends opposite do not seem to like this now, but a few years ago when there was another government in office, they were the ones who advocated what I am saying to-day and it was agreed that the government should not appoint the returning officers but that they should be appointed by the chief electoral officer and that he would try to select the best man possible and the one who would be fair to the various political opinions in each constituency. That was done at that time; the system worked well, and to change it now is, I am afraid, a breach of faith. It means that my hon. friends opposite when they are in opposition will ask their opponents to agree to changes which will ensure impartiality in the elections, but as soon as they are in office they repeal those laws and see to it that their own political friends are put in charge of an election. That is a wrong principle; it is a wrong thing to do, and I say again that it is a breach of faith on the part of those who have taken advantage of the agreement which was entered into between the parties a few years ago.

This is the clause which
provides for the appointment of returning officers. In order to make the matter clear may I just quote as briefly as I can a report of the chief electoral officer pursuant to section 74 of the Dominion Elections Act, made December 1, 1926, in the appendix of which he gave a summary review of the statutory provisions affecting from time to time the appointment and duties of returning officers. I am not quoting in extenso, because I do not wish to take up the time of the committee. He goes back to the British North America Act of 1867, section 42, where the governor general was empowered to issue a writ for the election of a member of the House of Commons to such returning officer in each electoral district as he thought fit, the person selected to conduct the election in accordance with the electoral law of the province in which lay the electoral district for which he was appointed. He goes on to say:
Under the first Dominion Elections Act, passed in 1874, the discretion thus given to the Governor General was taken away, and it was provided that the writ should issue to the sheriff or registrar of deeds for the electoral district or a portion of it. The Governor General had accordingly power to choose the returning officer at his discretion only in a district in which there was no sheriff or registrar or the incumbents of these offices were disqualified or unable to act.
Dominion Elections Act

The position in Canada was thus assimilated to that which then existed and has ever since existed in Great Britain, where the returning officer is always, ex officio, the sheriff, the mayor or the chairman of the local municipal council. This new rule, however, continued in force_in Canada for only eight years. In 1892, by 45 Viet. c. 3, s. 6, the Governor General was again given a discretion-
That is just another way of stating that the appointment was again put under patronage.
-whenever an election was required to be held in any electoral district, to select such person to act as returning officer as he thought fit, and this discretion he has continued ever since to exercise. ...
Until, in 1925, the law was amended in the way to be later mentioned, this power fell to be exercised only on the occasion of the issue of the writ for an election, and it was accordingly inevitable, even apart from the fact that the returning officer had a casting vote in case of a tie, that appointments should, as a general rule, be made, from among the political supporters of the government of the day; in practice each returning officer no doubt was chosen usually on the recommendation of the person or persons by whom the local party patronage was controlled. Though there were exceptions to this general rule, particularly when officers appointed by the provincial government, such as sheriffs or registrars were available to act and were willing to undertake the returning officer's duties, these were not numerous, and a secondary but very natural consequence of the established practice was that the returning officers selected their deputy returning officers from among their political friends, the names no doubt often being supplied from the same source as that from which the recommendation for the returning officer's own appointment had emanated. Again the general rule was subject to exceptions: in some electoral districts there grew up the practice of selecting half the deputies from each political party,-
And let it be remembered that the party led by my right hon. leader was then in power.
-this exceptional practice being no doubt usually confined to those electoral districts in which the returning officership itself was not looked upon as a party appointment. In most electoral districts, however, the political party in power had exclusive administrative control of the election.
... In 1925, however, the law on the last point was amended, it being provided that returning officers, instead of being appointed only for the purpose of conducting a particular election, should hold office during pleasure like other servants of the crown. The first returning officers appointed under the new provision were those who acted at the general election held later in the same year. When, nevertheless. a second general election was required to be held within less than twelve months, most of the appointments thus made wrere cancelled and new returning officers named instead of the original appointees.
Now we come to 1929. In spite of the fact that we on this side of the house were made

well aware by the actions of the majority of the persons representing the party now in power, of their manner of conducting elections, on representations made, especially by persons from the southeast corner, and acting on the recommendations of the chief electoral officer, the committee of 1929 of which I had the honour to be chairman, recommended that from then on the appointing of the returning officers should be taken out of the hands of political parties and placed in the hands of the chief electoral officer. I speak of this with some little feeling because at that time I was being constantly importuned. When we were sitting on the government side, I was being called into corners of the corridors and interviewed in my office and told time and again: You do not mean to say that you will make a recommendation that means that we may have a Tory returning officer, or a returning officer who will not be at our beck and call? I then took the attitude which I take to-day, that elections should be as far as possible taken out of politics. Day after day I was obliged to fight the men of my own side o<f the house, some of them very important men, in order to press the amendment through. I was told at that time by one after the other that if through some mischance the hon. gentlemen who now sit opposite came into power they wmuld see to it that the election act was changed so that it would go back to the good old, bad old, days of patronage. In view of the representations made, in view of the concession if I may so call it, although it was not a concession, it was an amendment made in the interests of justice and fair dealing, in view of the action of one party, I took it upon myself to say I was convinced that for all time in Canada we would take elections out of politics. Unfortunately no sooner had hon. gentlemen opposite come into power than we began to discern that efforts would be made to change the returning officer. To-day, although I suppose that is not of much importance, but I feel somewhat humiliated, I have to face men from my own side of the house who make no bones about telling me they told me so. I think probably my leader feels very much the same way as I do, and that may account for the energy with which he opposes this bill.

We had an election act agreed upon by all parties in this house, which it was hoped would give a fair, reasonable and honest election, and according to the report of the chief electoral officer it did so. And may I say, in case it may be brought up later, that the power conferred on the chief electoral officer was used wisely and in the public interest. I have here a list of the appointments by occupation. (Simcoe): What was the agreement about deputy returning officers?

I do not know what happened in other cases, but in my own constituency I went to the Conservative ex-candidate, and we sat down together and agreed on a returning officer. His recomendation accompanied mine to the chief electoral officer, and during the progress of the election the Conservatives received the right to appoint fifty per cent of the deputy returning officers. That was my duty, as I conceived it, in carrying out an obligation which I had undertaken before the people of Canada.
That was not the case in my riding; I never had a look in.

I can only speak of my own case. Now let us see the reason for all this eagerness on the part of the government to dismiss returning officers and appoint those of their own choice. I received a statement from the chief electoral officer, after I had questioned him in the committee, to the effect that since 1930 with resignations, deaths and removals there had been changes in regard to fifty-three returning officers, and that under the redistribution act there would be sixty new returning officers. There were thirty new appointments made necessary due to returning officers being over the age of sixty-five, and three appointments made necessary by reason of the fact that the returning officer now resided outside of his electoral district. In other words approximately 150 of the 245 returning officers would be dismissed in any case. So all this upheaval, all this change in this act and the franchise act, came about, I am firmly convinced, for no other purpose than to see to it that every single returning officer who was not appointed by the Tories would be dismissed.
There is no doubt that the object was to take charge of the making of the electoral lists, which duty was formerly performed by the returning officers. I say in all sincerity that if, as has been stated by the chief electoral officer, the deputy returning officers could carry on their duties of making up the lists during the time of the election, if they had

Dominion Elections Act

a four year period when there was no election there was no reason why they could not have continued to carry on that work. Instead of that we are naming a whole host of officers to carry on the enumeration. I suppose the Minister of Justice knows as well as I do that something like eighty thousand officers are required to carry on the enumeration of an election, so during the course of this summer in this general registration something like eighty thousand people will be employed by this government, which is another way of bribing the electorate in addition to the public works program. The whole aim and object of these two thick, cumbersome bills was to get into the hands of the government control of the entire electoral machinery, from the time the man goes to register himself on the list until he goes to the poll to vote to put this government out of power. I do not think they will dare do anything to interfere after the ballots are counted.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that he should read the reports of the chief electoral officer of 1926 and 1930. I should like to quote from paragraph 11 of the report of 1926, in which the chief electoral officer says:
... the fact that appointments are generally made from among supporters of the party in power naturally inclines supporters of the opposite party to think that unfair administrative tactics are intended to be or are in fact resorted to.
To that statement I subscribe, knowing hon. gentlemen opposite.
In some eases, however, the present mode of the selection of election officers does induce on the part of appointees a mistaken idea that they owe a duty to the party to which they belong rather than to the state by which they are employed and paid.
I have nothing more to say on this matter; already I have taken up enough of the time of the house in connection with this legislation. Before I take my seat I should like to thank the minister for cooperating in the minor amendments which were made to the act, in our endeavour to make the act more workable. May I say at the same time, however, that the general principle underlying the act, whereby once more we are bringing the whole electoral machinery under party patronage, to be operated for the benefit of party politicians, to my mind is not a principle which should be adopted readily by this house, particularly when we have had a chance to get away from it and the people of Canada were given an opportunity to see that in some instances the political parties could come together in an endeavour to give to the electorate a fair

deal and an open, above board method of expressing their opinions when elections came on.
I submit that this legislation is in keeping with a great deal of the legislation that has been brought down by hon. gentlemen opposite. It has been said by adherents of and apologists for the government that they have not paid enough attention to the political side of administration, and that their acts have not been motivated by political consideration. May I say that in my humble opinion hardly one piece of legislation has been introduced in this house since 1930 that did not have a political motive and a political purpose back of it. The tariff measures of 1930 were pure politics; the marketing act of this year was pure politics, and the central bank act was pure politics. Ever since this government came into power the relief measures have been pure politics, and they have been administered in the same spirit.

The hon. gentleman is out of order.
I would ask him to confine his remarks to the bill under discussion.

The chairman calls me to
order for having strayed a little from the subject. May I say that if all these measures I have mentioned were pure politics the two pieces of legislation we have been considering, as well as the redistribution act of last year, were politics of a kind I could not describe without falling foul of you, Mr. Chairman. Undoubtedly they were of the Tory brand of politics, which they hope will bring them into power at the next election but which I know will not do so.

I have refrained from saying anything on the floor of parliament with respect to these acts, though I had considerable to do with endeavouring to make them as workable as possible. I am not going to cover any of the ground already covered by my colleague from Quebec South (Mr. Power) and my right hon. leader in our endeavour to have the amendments so constructed that they would work fairly as between all parties, but there is one aspect of this whole procedure that I have not been able to understand. I refer to the necessity for this double staff of officials. If in the opinion of the government the chief electoral officer was not carrying out his duty they had the power, both in this house and in the other chamber, to get rid of him. But what have we done here? We have gone to work and provided for two sets of officials, which seems to me entirely unnecessary. I have said so all the time we have been dealing

Dominion Elections Act
with these two acts. We have set up one group of officials with a chief known as a revising officer; his appointees are permanent officials who will work for a period of six weeks in the year at most. For the life of me I cannot understand why these same officials should not be the returning officers. Evidently, as my colleague has put it much better than I can, there is a desire on the part of the government to give to their political supporters in each constituency the right to name the individual who shall conduct the election, and they content themselves with leaving only the chief electoral officer as a permanent official. In my humble opinion there is no necessity in the world for those two sets of officers. In order to carry out their desire the government have adopted this circuitous route to arrive at their destination. So far as I am concerned the best treatment I ever received was from a returning officer appointed by a Conservative government, I refer to Mr. Wilson who conducted the election of 1926. I have not a word to say against him or against his officers, and if officials of that type are selected by my opponents I shall be satisfied. Again I do protest emphatically against doubling up officialdom in connection with carrying on elections. It is an expense which could easily be avoided. Let me say in passing that I am afraid we will find the proposed system a most cumbersome one. Not only that, but it will be very expensive to every candidate who may have to contest an election under the provisions of this legislation. While a yearly revision of the lists shortens the election period by a few weeks, the candidates and sitting members will be shouldered with a tremendous expense to see that the lists are properly drawn up.
All these years we have managed to get along in western Canada with enumerated lists, and so far as I know we have had a fair degree of satisfaction. The machinery was under the supervision of the electoral officer and the returning officers in the various constituencies. My protest, togther with those of other hon. members on this side of the house, is that there is no necessity on earth for the double-barrelled provisions in the two pieces of legislation we have been considering. While I have tried to see some virtue in the proposed procedure frankly I can see none. There is the exception, however, that no doubt everyone will welcome the shortening of the election period. But to establish two sets of officials when one set could do the whole work in a proper fashion seems to me to be a totally unwarranted expense.

I cannot but associate myself with the view expressed primarily by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). As in the case of other hon. members I base my convictions mainly on my own experience with the different forms of appointments, and the manner in which elections have been conducted. In passing may I express my appreciation of the extremely nonpartisan attitude displayed by the hon. member for Quebec South when he attributed nothing but the purest political motives to anything done by the government since they came into power. I have heard words more unkind than that used by hon. members in his section of the house.
The question it seems to me is a simple one: Shall the returning officer look upon himself primarily as a representative of one party, or shall he look upon himself primarily as a civil servant responsible to the state for the proper carrying out of his duties. I am aware that appointments by a party should not necessarily, in the extreme sense, be partisan appointments, but it leaves the door open for that to take place. In common with other hon. members I have had the misfortune to contest several elections. Without hesitation I will say that from the point of view of its administration on the part of the returning officer, by far the most satisfactory election was that of 1930. Upon that occasion there was no Liberal candidate in my riding, although the returning officer was not aware of that fact at first. There was a Conservative candidate running against me. I believe I can speak for the Conservative candidate as well as for myself when I say that we received absolute satisfaction. The whole work was carried out in the fairest possible way, and without any regard so far as we could see- and we were in a position to judge-for the interests of any party in the field or which might be in the field, as opposed to those of any other party. The returning officer, although of course originally a party man, took a view which I considered quite correct and one which should be held by the majority of right-thinking men. He said he was not appointed under the auspices of any party. That is, he was employed by the state to see that the people in that part of the country over which he had jurisdiction had an absolutely fair opportunity to express their views, whatever they might be. I did not know the politics of half the deputy returning officers appointed, and I am not certain that my Conservative friend knew. But we did know that practically without exception those men under
Dominion Elections Act

the instructions of the returning officer carried out their duties in an absolutely fair and impartial manner. As I said in the beginning, they carried out their duties in a fair manner, and gave far more universal satisfaction than I had experienced in any other election. When we had a system which appeared to be satisfactory, and when it has been proved not only to the satisfaction of hon. members belonging to the party in power by whom the appointments were made, but to others, that the elections were carried on satisfactorily to all parties concerned, it seems to me to be a retrograde step to go back to the system which obtained before that time, when it was not satisfactory, and to take the risk even if the returning officers did their duty and even if the government had the altruistic motives, of being branded throughout the country as having made an effort to do otherwise and to gain an unwarranted advantage.
I can only conclude as I started out, by saying that I associate myself heartily with the point of view primarily expressed by the hon. member for Quebec South, and I urge the government in their own interests, in the interests of clean elections and in the interests of the people, to think again before taking a step which I am persuaded will be a retrograde one.

quite evenly divided, but I heard no complaints. Most of the men who are now governing in this house are the men who were dominant in the party at that time. I must say it is a great disappointment to the people of the country as a whole to find that they have so totally changed their views as to what is fair play in regard to elections.

I want to say that I subscribe to all that has been said by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). Before 1926 we had adopted the principle of having an officer appointed by this house appoint the returning officers in connection with the elections. This was changed in 1926 when the so-called shadow government came into power. We returned to that system in 1930, and I do not agree with what has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite. From all the reports I have had from the province from which I come, that system has worked most satisfactorily. I did have complaints and there were some heartburnings on the part of some of my friends in the constituency when strong Conservatives were appointed as deputy returning officers, but so far as I know they did their duty quite properly. When the election was over there were no complaints whatever.
This government was elected under that system in 1930. In 1934 they come down with a franchise act in which they propose to perpetuate that system so far as the franchise is concerned. They propose to appoint a commissioner of franchise and he is charged with the appointing of the registrars of electors in the various counties. He does the appointing, not the governor in council. So far as the franchise is concerned, this government has adopted the idea of having an officer appointed by this house-supposedly independent-appoint the registrars of electors in the different districts. That officer is to be appointed, by this house which, as at present constituted, is made up of a majority of hon. members opposite. That officer is to make the appointments so far as the franchise is concerned, but in the same breath, at the same session, and on the same day, we are asked to pass a bill with regard to elections whereby the provisions which have been in the act since 1926 and under which an officer of this house appointed the deputy returning officers are to be repealed. This particular function is to be exercised by the governor in council. How can my hon. friends justify the difference in the two systems? For the franchise, the

Dominion Elections Act
registrars of electors are to be appointed by an officer of this house; for elections, the deputy returning officers are to be appointed by the governor in council.
This must be because the chief electoral officer was appointed by a house in which those of us on this side had a majority. Hon. friends opposite now intend to have it both ways. They are going to appoint a commissioner of franchise with their majority and are perfectly willing to have that officer appoint the registrars of electors. On the other hand, they are going to repudiate that principle when it comes to the elections act, and have the deputy returning officers appointed by the governor in council. I submit that my hon. friends cannot justify the difference in these two systems. As the hon. member for Quebec South has said, there must be some sinister motive in this change at this time, in this repudiation of a principle which has been found to work quite well and which my hon. friends are accepting in the Franchise Act. They refuse to accept this principle in connection with the elections act.

I should like to make perfectly clear what the record discloses as to the understanding given to the house by the minister at the time the dominion franchise bill was introduced. The resolution preceding the bill was introduced on June 13, and at that time the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) gave a statement to the house as to the purpose of the measure. This statement will be found on pages 3938 and 3939 of Hansard. I shall read only one paragraph as the rest is simply an elaboration. He said:
It has bean thought by the government that it would be well to devise some improved method to bring on a general or a by-election in this country in much less time than is necessary at present. The proposal is that the government introduce a bill for the purpose of establishing the franchise of electors for dominion purposes and at the same time of providing for the making and completion of voters' lists which shall be regularly revised and kept up to date and which shall be available at a moment's notice in any part of Canada should a general election or a byelection take place. Under the scheme which is contemplated by the motion now before the committee it is hoped a franchise and voters' list act may be passed through this house and that under the new legislation a general or a by-election may be held in not more than twenty-eight days and possibly in twenty-four or twenty-five days.
The succeeding paragraph elaborates those remarks. The minister then said:
Mr. Speaker, I have now made a general statement of the purpose of the bill which it is intended to introduce.
There was in all that the minister said at that time no indication whatever of an intention to deal with the general elections act. The minister stated that the elections act was really three acts in one, it was a franchise act; it was an act concerning the preparation of lists, and it was an act respecting the machinery of elections. He stated that so far as the franchise act was concerned, he proposed to leave it as it was with the exception of the provisions respecting Doukhobors in. British Columbia. He stated also that he intended to leave the elections act as it was. Having in mind what had been said at the conference when the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) and myself met the Minister of Justice and the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan), I gave to the house what I gathered was the intention of the government. My hon, friend has intimated that the present elections is really three measures combined in one, that it is an act with respect to the franchise, an act with respect to the preparation of voters' lists, and also an act with respect to the machinery for the conduct of the elections themselves. speechtext: The bill provides that the franchise commissioner shall at once take steps and within six months have all the machinery going and the revising officers appointed. Before the bill is read the third time I wish to bring to the attention of the house a provision which I think should be included in this measure. An attempt has been made in the bill to make it as easy as possible, within certain limits, for individuals to exercise the franchise, and this was further added to yesterday in committee when the Minister of Justice introduced section 99 which provided for absentee voting. That section provides that fishermen, miners, lumbermen and sailors may vote by use of the absentee ballot if on election day they are not in the riding in which they are registered or within twenty-five miles of the constituency.
During the last few years there has been a development in the life of this country through which there are other people besides those actively engaged in the occupations mentioned who are compulsorily taken away from their homes-I refer to the men in the unemployment relief camps. If we refer to those mentioned in the category as entitled to vote by use of the absentee ballot we find fishermen, miners, lumbermen and sailors enumerated, and they are allowed that privilege because on election day they may not be in the constituency in which they are registered or within twenty-five miles thereof.
Let me give a hypothetical case. Let us say that in the city of Vancouver two men are looking for work prior to an election. One gets work in a lumber camp and goes there and on election day, if he is not within twenty-five miles of Vancouver, he is entitled to vote by use of the absentee ballot. The other man finds it impossible to get work and by force of circumstances he has to go into an unemployment relief camp; and because of that, although he is registered, these camps being more than twenty-five miles outside the city, he is unable to exercise the franchise. I hold that this is a discrimination of the worst kind against a man who, through no fault of his own, finds it

Dominion Elections Act
impossible to obtain work. I submit that those in the relief camps should be put in the same position as those enumerated in the category and who are unable to vote in the riding in which they are registered. Provision was made in bill 101 so that unemployed men away from home would not lose their franchise, but unless we make provision also for them to exercise it-and we have not made that provision so far-extending the franchise to them will be useless. To remove that discrimination I move, seconded by Mr. Mitchell:
That this bill be not read a third time now but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house with instructions that they have power to amend section 99, subsection (1), by adding after (e) a new clause (f):
"Unemployment relief camp workers" means all workers at any unemployment relief camp or at any institution or refuge maintained either by public or private moneys for the relief of distressed or unemployed persons.
And in subsection (2) after the word "sailor" in the fifth line, the words "or unemployment relief camp workers."
I have used these words because they are used in bill 101, rule 9, to make provision for the exercise of the franchise by men in unemployment relief camps. I hope that the house, as a matter of justice to those men who are so unfortunate as to be unemployed at this time, will see its way clear to adopt the amendment. The men in the unemployment relief camps are to-day continually informed that it is impossible for them to change the economic order in this country by means of our democratic institutions. If we do not include this amendment, if we expressly leave them out, we are giving proof positive to them that such is the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When the bill was before the special
committee appointed by this house, this question was very fully discussed and it was then that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) made his suggestion about absentee voters. He was not a member of the committee but was present during most of our sittings and heard what took place. After he made the suggestion in regard to absentee voters this clause was again discussed very thoroughly, and my recollection is that the committee was unanimous in confining the suggestion to fishermen, sailors, miners and lumbermen. It may be that there was one dissenting voice; it may have been seven to one but I think it was unanimous. Immediately applications came in from members of the house to include farmers, fruit pickers, teachers and various others. Well,
we felt that if we were going to adopt this provision at all we would have to confine it within some bounds and we confined it to those trades whose members we know go far away from home in response to the demands of their occupations. They have to go far from home and they might ordinarily be deprived of their vote unless some amendment of this kind were prepared. It was the opinion of the committee-and I am going to say it was unanimous, but it may not have been-that this should not be extended.
The question came up again when the matter was before the committee of the house yesterday and I expressed the same view as I hold now, that I would not be inclined to extend the provision. I understand that in some of the relief camps there are very few men belonging to the province in which the camps exist and they cannot take advantage of the clause in any event because it is confined to polling divisions within the province. It was suggested also that it might be broadened out that a man in a relief camp in Ontario might be permitted to cast his ballot down in Nova Scotia. We could not agree to that proposal and I do not accept it now.
I would like to ask the minister a question. There is trouble sometimes in connection with military camps; will any arrangement be made about those?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are covered in the act now; they were covered in the old act and we have not changed that clause.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I believe all hon. members will hope the relief camps are temporary institutions and not permanent or likely to be permanent. The insertion of a clause of this kind is suggestive of the possible permanency of relief camps. That phase of the matter I feel makes it undesirable to include an amendment of this nature. On the other hand when such a large number of men are in relief camps at the present time and when it is probable that this large number will continue to be in relief camps at the time the next general election occurs, I believe for the purposes of the next election it would be eminently right and just to have this particular clause included. If it were inserted in the bill at this time it could be repealed subsequently if the country found it possible through improvement of economic conditions to be freed of relief camps. I for one, should I be in a position so to do, would seek to bring about such a repeal subsequently if the conditions of the country so permitted. But,

Dominion Elections Act
with conditions as they are at the moment,
I shall lend my support very gladly to the inclusion of this amendment.
I wish to take advantage of speaking on the third reading of this bill to touch again on the question I asked the Minister of Justice a moment ago as to the preparation of the lists and the intention of the government to begin at once on their preparation. The minister replied that it was intended that the franchise commissioner should begin at once with the appointment of the franchise officers and the preparation of the lists. He mentioned that the act gave the commissioner a limit of six months within which to make the necessary preparations. Personally, I think that six months part of the measure is pure bluff. I believe it has been so provided to have it appear that we are not likely to have a general election during the remainder of this year. It is equally true, however, that the law has been so drafted as to enable basic lists to be prepared inside four weeks or, at the outside, six weeks. I hope all who feel as I do about the present administration will take care to see that within the next six weeks they become as busy as they oan to have the lists made as complete as possible.

May I say just a word as the seconder of the amendment. I do not think these men in relief camps are any different from the soldiers at the war and if I remember aright, provision was made for the exercise of the soldiers' franchise. I believe these men were forced away from their surroundings in just the same manner as were the soldiers and sailors. After all is said and done, the government of this country instituted these camps and in view of that fact they have a responsibility to see to it that nothing is placed in the way of these men exercising their franchise. It must also be remembered that owing to the low wages they are paid, it is impossible for them to return to their home towns or their places of origin in order to vote, and I see no reason why provision should not be made which will enable these men to take their part in the next election.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that these relief camps are temporary institutions. That does not alter the argument. While they may be temporary, as we hope they are, as a matter of fact they exist and an obligation rests upon the government, in view of their direct responsibility in the management of the camps, to see to it that these men are given an opportunity to exercise the franchise.

On section 12

Intimidation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This was my oversight, I am sorry to say. For many years the Trades and Labour Congress have requested that a clause which was formerly in the criminal code, in regard to picketing, should be restored or that the English clause in regard to the same matter should be incorporated in our law. Attending at or near or approaching to such house or other place as aforesaid in order merely to obtain or communicate information shall_ not be deemed a watching or besetting within the meaning of this section.
This was the law until the statutes were revised in 1896, when it was dropped without any repeal by this house. Of course the effect of the passage of the revised statutes would operate as a repeal.
