The house resumed from Thursday, June 28, consideration in committee of Bill No. 113, to provide for the construction and improvement of certain public works and undertakings throughout Canada-kMr. Stewart (Leeds)- Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 6-Tenders.

When the committee was last considering this bill we were at section 6. I had asked that sections 6 and 7 be considered together, because I felt that if old

Public Works Construction
section 36 of the Public Works Act were substituted for those two sections we would have a much better act and one which, with regard to draftsmanship and the possibility of being understood, would be very much superior to what we have at the present time. I understand that the minister is not agreeable to considering the two sections together, so I wish to withdraw the amendment which I proposed, making sections 6 and 7 one section, and to move that section 6 be amended by adding the words "by public advertisement" after the word "tenders" in line 4. It is not necessary for me to enlarge upon the advantage of doing that. We are now embarking upon a program of public works such as we have never had in this country before, and from the protection that is thrown around the expenditure of that money we are removing a safeguard that has existed ever since we had a public works act in this country. At this stage of the session I do not propose to elaborate on the advantage of receiving public instead of private tenders; that must be known to every hon. member of this house. Therefore I beg to move the amendment I have already read, and which I have placed in your hands.

The other day the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) brought up a very important question; he suggested that tenders should be confined to the particular localities where the public works are to be undertaken and that local contractors should be given the preference over contractors from outside the city or particular place where the public works were to be carried on. I would go a little bit further; I would suggest not only that local contractors should get the contracts but that those who are unemployed should be given work on these public works rather than men who already have employment. Therefore I would ask the Minister of Public Works if these contractors getting contracts will cooperate to the fullest degree with the representatives of such municipal relief authorities in order to make the works most effective in relieving unemployment. I believe these municipalities are very anxious to cut down relief costs, and certainly this is one way of putting to work a great many of the unemployed throughout Canada.
Amendment (Mr. Elliott) negatived on division.
Section agreed to on division.
On section 7-Cases in which tenders may not be required.

I have a complete change which I desire to move in regard to this section. The amendment is as follows:
That section 7 be deleted and that the following section be substituted therefor:
7. In case of work of pressing emergency in which, in the opinion of the governor in council, delay would be injurious to the public interest, or in which, from the nature of the work it could be more beneficially executed under the direct supervision and control of the officers and employees of the department in charge of such work, the governor in council, on the recommendation of the minister of such department accompanied by a certificate of the chief engineer or chief architect of such department or of the chief engineer or chief architect of the Department of Public Works, may direct that the work proceed forthwith without inviting tenders. Provided that in case of any one work the cost of which is estimated to be less than five thousand dollars, the minister or department in charge of such work may proceed with such work under the direction of such minister or department.
The object of this amendment is to make the section more workable. The bill now provides that tenders must be invited in every instance. There will be a large number of works costing less than $5,000, and every tender would have to be brought before the governor in council. Under the Public Works Act as it exists to-day, works under $5,000 may be let without tender, and I am therefore making that exception. Everything has to go before the governor in council, except works under $5,000.

You are just
embodying the present provision.
In that respect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But it goes farther.
Is the minister cutting out the word "economically"?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and putting in the word "beneficially."
Beneficial to whom?
To the public.
That ought to be said.

I had indicated to the minister that I intended to move an amendment which in many respects would be the same as the amendment he has now moved. I am wondering just why the words "expeditiously and economically" have been deleted, and the word "beneficially" substituted therefor. I think the effect is quite clear. The economical
Public Works Construction

end is not quite so satisfactory as the beneficial end, to the framers of the bill. I assume there is a good and sufficient reason behind making the change.
I will explain it.

In accepting the suggestion I made the other day in connection with tenders under $5,000, the minister is taking a step in the right direction. I am glad he has seen the error of his ways, and I trust that at a later part of the bill he will not move another amendment, which I understand he has in mind, which would negative the good effect of the amendment he has just moved. I hope he will not kick over the milk pail which he has filled, in an attempt to amend a subsequent section.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 8-Assistants.

I suggest that the minister ought to delete the words "and other persons." The section reads:
For the purposes of this act, the governor in council may authorize the minister charged with the execution of any work under this act from time to time to employ such architects, engineers and other persons as may be required'.
The expression "other persons" might include all sorts of people, and the effect would be that the money could be distributed among any number of persons-another election device as I see it.

The object is to cover the employment of foremen, supervisors, draftsmen, clerks and even messenger boys who are in charge of binding plans, and so on. I think the section should stand as it is. There is no intention to expand it any more than is absolutely necessary, and it is stated that we must go to the governor in council for authority.

It looks to me like an election device.

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 19, to incorporate the Bank of Canada.
He said: The first amendment deals with subsection 1 of section 5, which is amended by adding to the end of the subsection the words, "who shall not as such be a member of the board." That refers to the assistant deputy governor, and I see no reason why it should not be concurred in.
The second amendment is in section 6 where the word "financial" has been substituted for "banking." The section would then read, "the governor and deputy governor shall be men of proven financial experience." I would think that that was an improvement.
The third amendment deals with subsection 3 of section 8 where the words "subject to the approval of the governor in council" are added after the word "shall." I suppose there can be no objection to that.
The fourth amendment is in section 9, subsection 5, where the word "reelection" is substituted for the word "reappointment" I think reelection is proper.
The fifth amendment is in section 10, subsection 2, line 3. The Senate proposes that the following words be added:
. .. and any person nominated for election as a director who is a shareholder of a chartered bank shall if elected divest himself of ownership of his shares within three months of the date of his election and shall not thereafter during the period of his office have an interest, either directly or indirectly, as a shareholder in a chartered bank.

Bank of Canada
I believe the English system is to permit a lapse of time after the date of election, either to acquire the necessary qualifying shares or to divest of shares which should not be held.
I fail to see how a director of a bank could become a director of this bank, since he is prohibited from obtaining shares.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is exactly my view. The point being made by the Senate is that a holder of shares in the Bank of Canada who is also a holder of shares in a chartered bank might be elected, and this is to give him a chance to divest himself of his shares, in order that he may have no interest in a chartered bank while serving as a director. If I had my way about it I would add these words, "and until such time as he has divested himself of such shares he shall not act as a director." That would be the logical and proper wording to add.
The sixth amendment is in section 21, paragraph (i). It is proposed to add after the word "banks" the words "or to banks incorporated under the provisions of the Quebec Savings Banks Act." This amendment will have the effect of authorizing and empowering the Bank of Canada to make loans to a bank incorporated under the provisions of the Quebec Savings Banks Act. There are only two such banks, one at Quebec and one at Montreal. I cannot speak with great certainty about the bank at Quebec, but the one at Montreal is in as excellent a condition as any chartered bank in Canada.

Are these
provincial institutions?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is the old act which I think had its origin in pre-confederation days. The Montreal District and Savings Bank and La Caisse d'Economie de Notre Dame de Quebec are incorporated under the provisions of this statute. I suppose there is no reason why the Bank of Canada should not lend to either one of these banks if they desired a loan.
The seventh amendment is in paragraph (m) of the same section. It will be observed that in the third line of that paragraph the word "savings" has been used. The word "Quebec" is being added, so that it will read "incorporated under the Quebec Savings Bank Act." The word "deposits" is spelled with a capital "D", and this should be a small "d".
The next amendment is in section 27. It is proposed to add the following as subsection 7:
Every bank incorporated under the Quebec Savings Banks_ Act shall maintain against its deposit liabilities such reserves in the form of notes of the bank or deposits with the bank or a chartered bank as may be deemed to be necessary by the bank, and shall furnish such information as may be required by the bank from time to time to satisfy it that such reserves are so maintained.
It is within the mind of the house that the question whether or not the two institutions I have named should come within the provisions of this bill was discussed in the committee and I think in the committee of the whole house. If my memory serves me aright, it was stated that if these banks desired to avail themselves of the provisions of this bill, they should make the same deposits as the chartered banks. As the subsequent sections anticipate that the gold of these two banks is necessarily to be transferred to the Bank of Canada, and as the reserve now provided for in subsection 7, which is added, provides that the reserves shall be to the satisfaction of the Bank of Canada, but may be kept partly in the Bank of Canada and partly in the chartered bank, that difficulty is overcome. But personally I have doubts as to whether or not the bank should be permitted to keep any part of its reserves in a chartered bank, because the theory of the statute is that the chartered banks themselves must keep their reserves with this bank; and therefore any bank that avails itself of the benefits of the Bank of Canada Act should also accept the responsibility of keeping its reserves either in the form of notes of the bank or in the Bank of Canada itself. I suggest therefore that the words "or a chartered bank" should be deleted from the amendment made by the Senate for the reasons I have indicated.
The next, No. 10, is found in section 36 and is one in which I think the house can concur. Subsection 4 reads:
The voting of the shareholders shall be by ballot.
The Senate proposes to add, after the word "shall," the words "in the case of the election of directors"-obviously, in my judgment, a very proper correction. And in the twelfth line of the same subsection the Senate proposes to delete the words "by registered post," taking the view that to provide that in every case the writing should be transmitted by registered post might create confusion and difficulty. So that, instead of
Bank oj Canada

reading as it does in the bill that went from this house, it would read:
No person shall vote by proxy except that any shareholder may give to the minister, in writing, instructions as to the manner in which he desires to vote on any business of the meeting.
The words "by registered post" are deleted on the ground that it might cause confusion and difficulty. Personally I cannot see the point, but I have no objection.
Originally, was it intended to limit voting by ballot to the election of directors?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The point is as to
whether the letter shall be registered or not.
But originally, was it the intention to restrict the voting of shareholders to voting by ballot on the election of directors?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, because that is the only thing that the shareholders do, and it was intended always that these words should be implied rather than stated. That is the implication, because there are few cases in which the shareholders would have necessity for voting.
The last amendment will be found in section 43, by adding to paragraph (d) of subsection 1 the following:
And such by-laws may provide for the nomination of directors before any annual general meeting and what constitutes such nomination.
That is a very admirable addition because, as it read, it might be necessary to imply it rather than to have any direct authority as to the manner in which directors should be nominated. We can concur in that also. I would move therefore that we concur in amendment No. 1, in section 5, "who shall not as such be a member" of the board- that is, the assistant deputy governor shall not be.

Did that refer to the
deputy governor or the deputy minister of finance?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The assistant deputy
governor. In my opinion it means that now, because, unless there is specific provision that does make him such, he is not anyway; and inasmuch as it is not specifically provided, he is not. But the Senate has added those words.
The deputy minister and the assistant deputy governor, both appointees of the government, will have no vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

The only
votes on the board which the government directly controls by way of appointment are the governor and the deputy governor.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is No. 1, and I
move that we concur therein. No. 2 is the substitution of the word " financial" for "banking," which is an improvement, leaving a doubtful question muoh clearer than it was. No. 3, at the foot of page 3, adds after the word "shall" in the third line, subsection 3, the words "subject to the approval of the governor in council" dealing with the question of salaries. I think it is a 'proper safeguard, and I move that we concur in that one also. The fourth amendment substitutes for the word "appointment" the word "election," and I move that we concur in that amendment, because "election" is an accurate statement and "appointment" inaccurate. The fifth amendment deals with the question of the director elected, who owns chartered bank stocks, divesting himself of them in a period of three months. It seems to me that the logical thing to do would be to provide that until he has divested himself of such shares he shall not act as such director.

Or the board would be
short in the meantime.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the board would be short. I am entirely in the hands of the house with respect to that, but I think we can leave it as it reads; it will not make any difference. The next amendment in which we can concur is No. 6, on page 10, paragraph (i) of subsection 1 of section 21, making the act apply to the Quebec Savings Bank Act, to which there is no objection, and adding the words "of Quebec" before the word "savings" on the sixth line on page 11, as well as making a capital "D" a small "d" in the word "deposits." I move that we concur in these six that I have just indicated, because I want to speak specially as to the next one.
The first six amendments read the second time and concurred in.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The seventh amendment, at the end of section 27, reads:
Every bank incorporated under the Quebec Savings Bank Act shall maintain against its deposit liabilities such reserves in the form of notes of the bank or deposits with the bank

Bank of Canada
or a chartered bank as may be deemed to be sufficient by the bank, and shall furnish such information as may be required by the bank from time to time to satisfy it that such reserves are so maintained.
Does "the bank" there mean the central bank?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. I apprehend that the reason for this is that the chartered banks will pay some small interest on deposits made by the savings bank. The Bank of Canada has none. I apprehend that whoever was responsible for the amendment contemplated the possibility of some interest being received.
I will state the case for this amendment and I will state the case against it. In favour of this amendment, which is the logical and complementary amendment, to guarantee all the privileges of the central bank to the savings banks, that is the maintenance of reserves, is to be found this: that they shall be maintained in such a way as to be deemed sufficient by the Bank of Canada. That, I take it, would enable the governor of the Bank of Canada to say: We are not satisfied with the size of your deposit in a chartered bank and therefore you will have to increase your deposit with this bank despite what you have in the chartered bank. Against that is this: the chartered banks themselves are compelled to maintain reserves and it is not the general spirit of the statute that one of the institutions which is permitted to carry on business with the central bank should be maintaining a portion of its reserves with one of the banks that has itself to carry on its business in the way indicated. The other answer in favour of the amendment is this: that inasmuch as any chartered bank that receives a deposit is compelled by law to have a deposit with the central bank, there is inferentially a twofold security, that is the security made by the chartered bank that has the deposit as well as the security of the reserve in notes held by the savings bank to the satisfaction of the Bank of Canada.
As the Bank of Canada is in control, could it not ask for an increased deposit?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is my judgment. Unless there is some reason in the minds of the house why we should disagree, after looking at the matter from every angle, in view of the fact that the deposit made by the savings bank with a chartered bank will have in itself to be covered by a deposit in the central bank, that makes the matter perfectly secure.

Would it not be quite satisfactory for these two banks for which provision is being made, to be governed in their borrowings from the central bank by the same regulations that govern the chartered banks?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are. The only addition is this: hon. members will recall that among the powers that the bank may exercise is that of lending money to chartered banks and this puts the savings banks in exactly the same position as the chartered banks, so the only question for consideration is really whether a reserve partly maintained in a chartered bank but in every instance to the satisfaction of the governor of the central bank, is adequate. Frankly, in view of the fact that the chartered bank must maintain its reserve for that deposit, we are quite safe in accepting the amendment.

The only other point about the matter is that I think the method of requiring a reserve from these Quebec savings banks is perhaps more scientific than that which we adopted in the bill itself in providing for a rigid reserve. I am strongly in favour of this kind of provision for a reserve, namely, one which the central bank may increase or decrease as the exigencies of the case demand. That seems to give a better control of credit than to have a fixed reserve of five per cent.
I am in favour of the amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have
been good enough to let us carry on this discussion so as to expedite business. I quite realize the fact mentioned by the hon. member, but there are certain circumstances, to which attention need not now be directed, that arose out of the operations of the Finance Act and of the banks whereby their reserves are at a low figure relatively to the position in England where ten per cent is the figure for large banks, six per cent being in notes of the Bank of England and four per cent being in deposits in that institution. In this instance, when we say "not less than five per cent", we are giving the banks substantial leeway in view of the fact that part of that may be carried in notes of the central bank.
The question is: Shall we accept the amendment? I see no reason why we should not unless there is some reason given against it.
Carried.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The other amendments
I think I have sufficiently explained as to the changes which are not important and which, I believe, are in the interests of the bill itself.
Franchise Commissioner

With regard to the surrender of gold, there is no provision for these banks surrendering gold. I do not know whether they have any or not, but I assume they have some. Is it intended that they shall surrender it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The bill says: "every
chartered bank shall", and they are chartered banks within the meaning of the statute. The words "chartered bank" means a bank to which the Bank Act applies.
Has the Quebec Savings bank any gold?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It probably has not. It might have a little. It is not a rule for it to carry any reserve of gold, but there have been cases in which, according to the bank returns, these two banks have had gold. The name is not the Quebec Savings bank. The banks have their existence under the provisions of the Quebec Savings Banks Act. One bank is the Montreal City and District Bank and the other is La Caisse d'Economie de Notre Dame de Quebec. I think it is contemplated that the gold would be returned over to the Bank of Canada.
I would therefore move that the remaining amendments be concurred in.
Motion agreed to; amendments read the second time and concurred in.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOHN THOMAS CONNOLLY THOMPSON, D.S.O.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOHN THOMAS CONNOLLY THOMPSON, D.S.O.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the
chair I would like to make a motion now that the franchise bill has been disposed of. I move:
That John Thomas Connolly Thompson, D.S.O., of the city of Ottawa, in the province of Ontario, one of His Majesty's counsel, learned in the law, be appointed dominion franchise commissioner in accordance with the provisions of an act respecting the franchise of electors at elections of members of the House of Commons.
I was going to ask my right hon. friend to second the motion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOHN THOMAS CONNOLLY THOMPSON, D.S.O.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
have much pleasure in seconding the motion which my right hon. friend has just moved. All who know him must regard Colonel Thompson as a man of the highest probity and integrity. His honesty and ability cannot

be questioned. I for one am prepared to believe that the qualities of character which have made him somewhat rigid in the work of administration of the particular commission over which he presides are characteristics of a strict impartiality and honesty of purpose which may give him a special fitness for this particular post.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOHN THOMAS CONNOLLY THOMPSON, D.S.O.
speechtext: May I draw the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that the legislation provides that the salary be fixed as well?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOHN THOMAS CONNOLLY THOMPSON, D.S.O.
speechtext: That was fixed this afternoon; it is in the bill and not in this motion.
Motion agreed to.

The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 113, to provide for the construction and improvement of certain public works and undertakings throughout Canada- Mr. Stewart (Leeds)-Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 9-Orders laid before house.

At six o'clock
I was speaking about an amendment that I wished to move to clause 9 which reads:
All orders in council made under the provisions of this act shall be laid before the House of Commons forthwith after the making thereof if parliament is then sitting, and if not, then within the first fifteen days of the next ensuing session.
This clause is similar to the one which has appeared in some of the acts respecting relief that have previously been passed, but it omits a very significant clause which is in the other relief acts, namely, that if parliament is not sitting such orders in council or regulations or an abstract thereof disclosing their essential provisions shall be published in the next following issue of the Canada Gazette. I ask the Minister of Public Works if he cannot see his way to include a similar additional clause to section 9, and to that end I would move:
That section 9 be amended by inserting after the word "then" in line thirty-nine, the words
"said orders in council or an abstract thereof disclosing their essential provisions shall be published in the next following issue of the Canada Gazette and laid before parliament.
I point out that this measure provides for a total expenditure of forty million dollars, and the greater part of it will be made before parliament reassembles. I think it is but reasonable to ask, particularly as the measure is one purporting to be for purposes of relief, that the same procedure should be followed

Public Works Construction
with respect to advising the country as to such orders in council as may be passed under this measure as has been followed with respect to orders passed under previous measures.

I submit that
this section as drafted is sufficient to meet the requirements of the situation. The activities of the government under this act are not of a special character such as those contemplated by the Unemployment Relief Act. In fact my right hon. friend and some of his followers have contended that many of these items might very well have appeared in the regular estimates of the department. The opposition have contended from time to time that they were prepared to vote practically any sum for the relief of unemployment as long as the government came before the house and gave particulars and details of the expenditures. This is not a blank cheque-
In spots it is.

Well, to a veiy
limited extent. It is an act authorizing the expenditure of specific amounts for particular purposes. There is nothing extraordinary or exceptional in its character. Therefore the reasons which prevail for publication of orders in council under the Unemployment Relief Act, which are of a special and exceptional character, involving activities outside the regular sphere of the work of the dominion government, do not apply to this. These are additional expenditures upon purely dominion undertakings. As my right hon. friend has said, they might perhaps properly appear in the regular estimates. If they had appeared in the regular estimates no one would suggest that any such provision should be inserted. A special provision has been inserted in the bill, section 10, providing that-
The Minister of Finance shall make a report to parliament within the first thirty days of each session during the currency of this act. containing a statement of all moneys expended under the provisions thereof and the purposes to which they were applied.
So I think we have anticipated to a very large extent the purposes which my right hon. friend has in mind. Let me compare that provision with what happens in the case of an expenditure in the regular way by the public works or any other department. These expenditures appear in the public accounts, but they would not be presented to parliament until the year following. We have anticipated that and provided that when parliament assembles we shall present a statement containing the details of these expenditures. They are not of an exceptional character, but are 74726-288
within the scope of the regular expenditures of parliament. It really is not necessary, I think, to go to the expense of publishing in the Canada Gazette a precis of orders in council with respect to the detailed expenditures. For these reasons I submit that the amendment is unnecessary and that every interest has been safeguarded by the provisions of the bill.

The reason
which was given by the minister is really amusing. It is quite funny. He says he does not think it is advisable to go to the expense of publishing a precis of these orders in council in the Canada Gazette. I suppose the cost of publication of a precis would amount to the cost of the setting of the type, because the rest of the cost would be the ordinary cost of getting out the Gazette in any event. It might come to ten or at the outside fifteen dollars an issue. I question if it would come to that. On the other hand the minister does not hesitate to ask us to vote forty million dollars for the purposes named in this bill. He asks us to vote that great sum for all kinds of purposes, and then he says it is rather too expensive to publish a precis in the Canada Gazette. I believe this measure-and I believe so more strongly than ever in view of what the minister has just said-is intended for election purposes. All these sums being appropriated are largely for the purpose of distributing money in different constituencies at a time just preceding an election. My belief is that an election will be held before parliament meets again, and the reason the minister does not wish to have any precis put in the Canada Gazette is that he does not wish the public to know how these moneys are being distributed. I say he must render himself open to that criticism and suspicion unless he is prepared to acquiesce in a very simple and obviously fair and reasonable amendment such as the one I have moved here.
Let me direct attention to the last item in the schedule to the bill:
To supplement where necessary specific amounts hereinbefore provided, upon the authority of the governor in council, $500,000.
That is half a million dollars just to be moved about in differing amounts at the pleasure of the governor in council. This will have to be done by order in council. Why should the public not know how much of that half million dollars is being paid out, when and where, and how much is going to one locality and how much to another? There is no defence for not being willing to acquaint the public with that. This talk about having

Public Works Construction

a report submitted to the next parliament is altogether beside the mark. It is meaningless. The public will want to know how this money which we are being asked to vote for relief purposes is going to be spent from month to month. The minister says that we were prepared to vote a large lump sum. That was always on the understanding that it would be accompanied with safeguards I am proposing which would ensure that the public be kept acquainted with the expenditure. And the attitude of the minister is the more unreasonable in that heretofore this has always been done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
I have in mind the bill passed at the last session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That was because there
were no details of the proposed expenditures. It was an estimate.

There are no
details of the half million dollars and other imounts here.

The wording of that item is taken from the wording of the regular estimates of the Public Works department year after year. It is an item that has appeared in the estimates of that department right along during all the years.

Then let us look again at schedule A; here is an item: Harbours and Rivers Generally

Improvements, maintenance of services, repairs and additions, $2,500,000.
Here is another: Interior department, $2,000,000. There is $4,500,000 just in a lump sum. That money will have to be spent, I assume, by orders of the governor in council. If not, it will be departmental expenditure previously provided for by order in council. If this is intended to help unemployment why should not the public have a precis from month to month? There can be only one answer, that the government is seeking to conceal the manner in which it will spend this money. I do not think we should allow this committee to report progress until we get satisfactory procedure on that point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I take it the right hon. gentleman desires to be fair. Will he give me any instance in which there has ever been any such provision as this inserted in the law, except where there was a general appropriation? I am just telling what happened. During the last days of his government he entered into a contract with respect to dredging in the St. Lawrence river, for instance, for which we

have had to provide money ever since, and which is not quite finished yet. We knew nothing of it and neither did the public, because there was an item in the estimates providing for dredging.
If you will be good enough to look at the schedule to this bill, Mr. Chairman, you will find that the name is given as to the location of every proposed expenditure. The half million dollars is merely to take care of the fluctuations that sometimes happen in connection with contracts. For instance, one of the contracts that came to this government as a legacy was in connection with a coffer dam in Saint John harbour, for which the contract price was so low that it was quite clear that it could not be built for that amount of money. The coffer d'am went out twice, and for extras that had been incurred before we assumed office it cost us more than the contract price. No one published a precis of that in the Gazette; it was never asked or suggested that this should) be done.
I suggest that if we are going to adopt this as a principle in this house it should be the subject matter of general legislation. I could start at Halifax and go straight through to Vancouver. For instance, I discovered only by accident that my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) had raised the salaries of charwomen a few days before the election.

That was understood
months before.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Certainly it was not published in the Gazette. Let us be fair with each other. Everything in this bill complies with the provisions that have obtained heretofore in connection with estimates. I will admit that there is one item of $2,000,000 in connection with the Department of the Interior, and a further item of $2,500,000 in connection with harbours and rivers generally. As I said to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) when he mentioned it the other day-and this was one of the matters that influenced the government in making the item so large-there have been severe storms on the Atlantic coast resulting in great destruction of wharves and breakwaters in the little harbours. We could not undertake to sipecify them all here; to do so would have been ridiculous, but this item will cover them. The reason the last section is in this bill is to enable parliament, just as soon as the house meets, to have full knowledge of what has been done. That is unusual, but because we have to spend money for these particular

Public Works Construction
purposes, owing to conditions to which the hon. gentleman very properly referred the other day, we have provided that this house shall be seized of all the steps that have been taken as soon as the house meets, which is unusual. Otherwise we would have to wait for the auditor general's report.
I hope hon. gentlemen opposite will be fair and will not ask us, because we are near prorogation, to do something which is unsound as a principle unless adopted as a new rale in connection with all public expenditures. The hon. gentleman asks that whenever an order in council is passed a precis of it shall be published in the Gazette. The rules require that matters dealing with public policy should be so dealt with but in this case just what would happen? In connection with this legislation, over a period of months, probably there would be three or four hundred orders in council. What would the precis amount to? "Contract let for an addition to a building at Kamchatka for $10,000; contractor, John Smith and Company." That would be all, and what purpose would be served by that? It never has been done before, nor has it been asserted that it should be done. I can only say that I think the right hon. gentleman's sense of fairness, when he looks at the schedule, will satisfy him that we have endeavoured to do what always has been done, and have gone just one step further. I may say that I accept the responsibility for that last section. I felt that with respect to those basket items, if I might call them such, we should give the fullest information at the earliest possible moment, and when the house meets the information will be supplied at once. I think probably that is about as fair a proposal as has ever been made in this house.
Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver); The election will be over then.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
prescience, I suppose, is very great in the sense that he is a Hielander, and no doubt always will have that second sight that is denied to other people, but it will be remembered that coming events cast their shadows before.

The Prime Minister cannot have it both ways. He can either say that these are ordinary items of departmental expenditure on public works and that the same policy should be followed with respect to them that is followed with respect to the items in the ordinary estimates, or he will have to take the ground, which he has taken up to the present, that these are all
74726-288J
exceptional expenditures, and that they are for the purposes of relief, in which event he ought to follow the procedure that has been followed in the past with respect to expenditures for relief. I am basing my attitude and argument on the allegation of the government that these expenditures are intended for relief purposes; it is so stated in the preamble of the bill. The Prime Minister made reference to what happened in the last session of the previous parliament, and I think he spoke of the items that were brought down before the election.	-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I was not complaining about that.

Evidently something of the kind is in his mind at the moment. My right hon. friend spoke about dredging in the St. Lawrence. I find here in the supplementary estimates presented a day or two ago an item of $1,000,000 for the St. Lawrence ship canal, dredging, and to provide for work performed and to be performed by contract. That looks like the eve of an election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is part of the legacy we inherited under that contract.
Mr. STEWART (Edmonton); Why did you not vote it in the main estimates?
Mr. BENNETT; Because most of the work has been done. The rest of it is with respect to the St. Augustine bar which is in front of the bridge coming up the St. Lawrence river.

This bill has
been referred to right along as a measure for the purpose of relief, and the preamble
says:
*-and whereas the construction and execution of the works mentioned in the schedule hereto will tend to increase employment and reduce expenditures for relief purposes-
That is the whole purpose of this measure, professedly. From the beginning I have said that I do not think such is the purpose at all but that the purpose is to put the government in possession of sums of money which they will be free to distribute all over the country. I think the public will be very much interested in knowing whether with its money John Smith and Company of such and such a village gets a contract of a certain amount just a few weeks before the election takes place; I think in other constituencies the public will be interested to know who secured the contracts that are let and sums paid out for all kinds of purposes. Unless that is what the
Public Works Construction

government are seeking to conceal why will not the minister come across in this and do exactly as he has done in previous relief measures?

I just want to direct the Prime Minister's attention to what really are the blank cheque items. On page 4 there is an item of $2,500,000 for harbours and rivers generally; improvements, maintenance of services, repairs and additions. An item of that size never has been voted before in connection with harbours and rivers. Here is another basket item, to use my right hon. friend's expression:
Interior Department-[DOT]
To provide for the construction and development of public buildings, camp sites, electric light and telephone systems, highways, trails, water and sewer systems, recreational areas, wharves, and river protection works; to provide for the development of historic sites including buildings repairs and restorations; also to provide for the construction of the Golden-Revelstoke (Big Bend) section of the trans-Canada highway between Golden and Canoe river, further to provide for the purchase and acquisition of building sites, $2,000,000.
That is spread clear across the Dominion of Canada, from Halifax to Vancouver. Then here is another item:
Indian Affairs Department-
For the reconstruction of Indian residential and day schools, and hospitals, $500,000.
That is spread across Canada as well. Then there is another item:
Public Buildings Generally-
Improvements, additions, fittings, repointing, painting, repairs and renewals to heating, floors, roofs, plumbing, electrical installations, improvement of grounds, sidewalks and roadways; and incidental expenditures in connection therewith, $2,000,000.
I submit that those are not ordinary items. There is another item on page 6 of the bill providing for an expenditure of $500,000. It is as follows:
To supplement where necessary specific amounts hereinbefore provided, upon the authority of the governor in council.
Those items are altogether different from the ones voted under the estimates. As is stated in the preamble, they are voted to effect national recovery. The actual words are "for the general advancement of the country and to accelerate recovery to more normal economic conditions". I submit that the Prime Minister ought to be fair, and-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will meet my right hon. friend in this regard. I am content that with respect to those items for which there are no particulars, this amendment should apply, but with respect to the others the normal pro-

vision in connection with estimates will be applicable. If the right hon. gentleman will arrange his amendment accordingly I shall meet him. I will say that with respect to harbours and rivers generally, the representations made by the hon. gentleman were not without some force in connection with conditions on the Atlantic, because I had a report, myself, as to the abnormal storms which had created those conditions. In connection with the item of $2,000,000 for public buildings I think the minister proposes to add to it the new constructions, because there are places in which the old buildings have to be torn down entirely, and new buildings put up. I shall be pleased now to meet the conditions stated by the right hon. gentleman, by providing that in all items other than those specifically mentioned the precis should be published in the Gazette.

In the circumstances I shall be prepared to accept the Prime Minister's offer. My amendment will then read:
That section 9 be amended by inserting after the word "then" in line thirty-nine, the words:
"Said orders in council or an abstract thereof disclosing their essential provisions shall be published in the next following issue of the Canada Gazette, and laid before parliament, in the case of all expenditures the amounts of which are not specifically set forth in schedule A."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am prepared to accept that.
Thank you.
Amendment agreed to.

Before the section is carried let us go back to January 2, 1931. I have before me a most admirable speech delivered in the city of Calgary about unemployment. It is reported in the Montreal Gazette. It is not very long, and this would be the most convenient time to-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the rule is that the hon. member is out of order, and perhaps it might as well be enforced to-night. I submit newspaper articles read for the purpose of influencing the action of parliament are and always have been out of order.

Speaking to the point of order, may I say that I have no intention of delaying the session. I would not make a long speech. I have tried to learn some speeches by heart. But according to the rules of the house, a number of which I know by heart, let me tell you that it is permissible for a member to quote any speech delivered outside the house. The speech I shall read was not delivered by Abraham Lincoln at

Public Works Construction
Gettysburg, but was delivered by the right hon. Prime Minister in his own constituency of Calgary. It is headed "Bennett Plans Move to Avoid Future Slump. Is Not Satisfied with Temporary Relief."
What is the date of it?

January 2, 1931. The heading continues with the words "Seeks Final Causes." Then, this is a most important point -I am coming to it: Very often in this house I have asked the Minister of Labour to make a classification of the unemployed, in order to cure unemployment. I was delighted to hear the Prime Minister answer one question this year, after the numerous questions which for four years I have been asking. He answered that the government was doing its best to classify the unemployed.
Order.

And, sir, I quote this
because I am sure that on that occasion the Prime Minister was right. I fully agree with what he said, but the trouble is that he afterwards changed his mind. What he said in Calgary on January 2, 1931, is O.K. He spoke as a statesman, and I did not have an opportunity to congratulate him. I began to congratulate him one day after I had spoken in a debate prompted by the hon. member for Bellechasse. I rose to speak, and I was about to congratulate the Prime Miinster when the house adjourned. Here is the quotation, by the Canadian press:
Order. We are discussing section 9.
Yes, sir.
I must ask the hon. member to make his remarks as relevant as possible.

Just a minute, sir. May I say just one thing before you give a final decision. Section 9 reads:
All orders in council made under the provisions of this act shall be laid before the House of Commons forthwith after the making thereof if parliament is then sitting, and if not, then within the first fifteen days of the next ensuing session.
This section refers to orders in council. The orders in council express the policy of the government with respect to relief of unemployment. Therefore, sir, when I quote the excellent speech delivered in Calgary by the Prime Minister with regard to unemployment, stating his policy at that time to end unemployment, I am perfectly within the rules. I am quite in order because the orders in
council mentioned in section 9 are supposed to contain the government's policy on the relief of unemployment. For these reasons I submit I am perfectly in order.
I do not criticize that speech. I eulogize it, I praise it, and I am sorry that the policy indicated therein has not been the policy followed by the government. I read:
Calgary, January 2. Application of temporary measures to correct present economic conditions will not satisfy Premier R. B. Bennett.
Order.
Order.

He is determined to unearth the final causes of the present depression and lay a secure foundation for permanent future prosperity. So he told' a large gathering of his fellow citizens of Calgary assembled to-day at a luncheon arranged jointly by the board of trade, the young men's section of the board of trade, and the Kiwanis club.
The	CHAIRMAN	(Mr.	Smith,	Cumberland) : Order, order.

"I cannot make up my mind" he said, "why this country between the lake and the mountains should experience the depression, why people who have lived here for years should now find themselves without any accumulation of goods, sometimes without the bare necessities of life."
The	CHAIRMAN	(Mr.	Smith,	Cumberland): Order. I wish to call the hon. member's attention again to the section under discussion, and the fact that what he is reading is not, in the opinion of the chair, in any way relevant to this section. I declare his remarks out of order.

I am sorry that the chair is wooden and wrong.
The	CHAIRMAN	(Mr.	Smith,	Cumberland) : Order.
Withdraw.

It is an insult to the Prime Minister. How can	we praise the Prime
Minister, when we are prevented from doing it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Name him.
The amendment has been revised in accordance with the agreement with the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, it is accepted.
Section as amended agreed to.
Public Works Construction

On section 10-Report to parliament.
On this section I would criticize the Prime Minister.
Order.
I am very sorry, sir, that those admirable statements made at Calgary have been forgotten. That was admirable; everyone agreed with it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it would be disastrous in the closing hours of the session if we should have to take action provided by the rules to deal with the hon. member for Temiscouata. I hope he will not make it necessary for the leader of the house to take action to that effect. I can say only this, that when the ruling of the chair is given we expect it to be obeyed.

Well, sir, on the point of order: The first part of the discussion was on another section, which has been approved. Now I was about to make another speech, but as it does not seem to please the government I will take the first opportunity to make it outside the house.
Mr, MACKENZIE KING: This section is somewhat similar to the section in the previous relief act, but there is no section in this bill similar to section 11 in the latest relief act which relates to the duration of the act. I think the minister should add a section to the effect that this act shall expire on March 31, 1935, unless there is some special reason why that should not be done.

My right hon. friend will observe that several of these items are for the construction of large buildings which manifestly cannot 'be completed by that time. Many1 of the works contemplated will be completed but many of them will not. I submit that we should not limit the operation of the act to a time known to be insufficient for the carrying out of its provisions and the expenditure of money which is authorized. I might say the practice in other countries is to make an appropriation for the carrying out of a certain work without limitation as to .time.

Yes, but the minister knows that the practice in this parliament and in the British parliament with respect to public works is to vote what is necessary only for a fiscal year at a time. That is one of the ways in which parliament maintains its control over expenditures. There is no reason in the world why these expendi-

tures should not be subject to the same control on the part of parliament as all other departmental outlays. I see in this another election device in the desire to give out work which will run over as many years as possible and for which some subsequent government will have to meet the expenditure. I certainly think there should be some section to limit definitely the time for which these appropriations are to be made. If buildings are in the course of construction, a subsequent administration may vote what is necessary to continue the work.

Just to supplement what my right hon. leader has said:	The same
point was raised when the first relief act was being considered, and I do not think anyone knows as well as the minister in charge of this bill the evils which arose under that act. There is no reason in the world why an estimate should not lapse at the end of a fiscal year. Any reasonable estimate will be revoted by the house. Should a contract be let for large public works which expires on March 31, I think it can be assumed that the necessary money will be revoted provided a reasonable explanation is given. I do not think it is within the experience of any hon. member that such a course was not pursued. I submit that there should be a limit upon these things, and that limit should be mentioned in the bill.

I would point out that this is a special appropriation, the object of which is to provide employment over a considerable period of time. It is not in the nature of an ordinary supply vote; its purpose is well defined and well understood, to sustain employment over a period of a year or longer. Any termination of the act at any particular time would be calculated to defeat the object in view.

They are voting it now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend
will take trouble to listen he will have no difficulty in understanding the matter. In the first place the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart), who is sitting beside him, knows the conditions in Banff; he was Minister of the Interior. An opportunity is afforded to secure the old Brett sanatorium property for $20,000, the hotel having been burned. There is no administration building and no post office building in Banff. The town is visited by more people than is any other part of southern Alberta, and the complaints have been very numerous and have been directed against this government ever since we took office that we did not provide a post office and administration building. I felt that under normal conditions it was impossible to do so and this vote which has arisen because of the handing back to the people of the increased value that has come from gold has enabled a national park, which was in no sense looked upon as belonging to my constituency, to benefit. This was an opportunity to establish a decent administration building and a post office on a site that we should have had when the park was laid out, a site across the bridge on the main street of Banff. That is that.
Second, the retaining wall is being constructed because of the negligence of the right hon. gentleman's government. When he transferred the natural resources to the province, despite the protests that we made that he had not vested the waters in the province and had retained them for the dominion, he and his law officers persisted that they were right and we were wrong. They subsequently changed their minds and found out that we were right, that no steps have yet been taken to vest those waters in the province. This involves a very considerable difficulty because the Irrigation Act provides that those waters
Public Works Construction

are the property of the crown in the right of the dominion and the irrigation works that have been constructed lying east of Calgary, enhanced the flow' of water so that the bed has been eaten out by the scouring of the water until there is only a short distance between the water and gas and other pipes in that area. That explains the item, but it may interest my right hon. friend to know that the major part of the work is in East and not in West Calgary, the latter being my constituency. Very little and, in fact, I think under the new boundary none of it is in West Calgary.
The third item, that is the $1,200,000 is one about which I was quite confident that a person who has the attitude of mind of suspicion and distrust the right hon. gentleman has toward problems that affect public life would at once charge me with an effort to give to the constituency of Calgary more than it should receive. These are the facts: For long years the permanent force of this country has been seeking some permanent barracks. I believe the permanent force wd.ll continue to exist as long as governments exist in this country. It is a very small force but it serves to preserve the civil institutions of the dominion in times of civil disorder or insurrection or riot. It is essentially a police force for Canada. A unit of that permanent force has been in Calgary for some years but it has been so poorly housed it has bad to be reduced and it is occupying the armouries that belong to the non-permanent militia, greatly to their detriment and greatly to the detriment of the efficiency of militia headquarters. This work involves the construction of ten or eleven units and it cannot be done to supply accommodation for horses and men for less than that sum of money. Recently the city council by a majority protested against that work being constructed in Calgary and I asked the Minister of Works to provide that the item should read: "or elsewhere in the province of Alberta." That is that that work should be constructed in the province of Alberta which is to be the home of a unit of the permanent force. That is the explanation of the item. Because that has been done it is charged that I have been guilty of many offences in endeavouring to remedy an injustice that has been done to the permanent force for the last ten years, because wherever the barracks are, the permanent force will be. If the building is not in Calgary, the permanent force will go somewhere else. That is the position.

We tried
to get it to Edmonton.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have no doubt as to that. But the necessity for the work was the only factor that governed in any of these matters. When the right hon. gentleman referred to the estimates of 1930 he must have known first of all that the public building is not in my constituency. That is number one. Number two is that in 1912 the government of that day acquired the site but the post office building, which it is, was erected originally on lots given to the crown by citizens of Calgary, the other lots being bought, and the site on the corner of Second street east and Eighth avenue was acquired in 1912 with a frontage of 250 feet on Eighth avenue. The contract was let and the sum of $1,000,000 in the estimates was to pay the contractor for the completion of the building which was completed in the fall of 1932. That is the story.
It seems to be idle to endeavour to induce hon. members opposite to believe there are those still living in this country to whom the question of public necessity is the governing factor in determining how money shall be expended. In this case there was necessity and no man knows the necessity better than does the hon. member for West Edmonton with regard to an administration building and a post office at Banff. Those who have read the press of that community and the criticisms made of successive governments because of lack of accommodation will understand what I mean.
With respect to the scouring of the Bow river and the wash-off of the water power, as I told my colleagues, unless we still owned that river, we would not for a single moment suggest that the work be done. On the other side of the river, as relief works were erected riprap works; we are doing this to supplement them and the majority of the work is in East Calgary.
As I said before, wherever the barracks are erected they are for the unit of the permanent force that must be housed and stabled somewhere west of Winnipeg. Thus far that unit has been in Alberta. This proposal is at my suggestion that the minister should move that there should be added the words: "or elsewhere in the province of Alberta."

The right hon. gentleman says that some of these items are due to the neglect of the previous administration and are necessary to fulfil an obligation outstanding for ten years. Why then was this not done in the first or the second or the third session or the fourth session while the Prime Minister has been at the head of the administration? Why do these items com!

into this bill just before prorogation, at this last moment of what I believe is the last session of this parliament? This item of $1,200,000 for a barracks is one that ought to have appeared in the Public Works estimates and should not have appeared in any measure that relates to purposes of relief.
I want to take exception to these enormous sums for military and police purposes being voted under the pretext of relief.
Oh, oh!

Hon. members say'"oh, oh;" Have they read the schedule? Look at the large items in this schedule, for military and police purposes: Calgary barracks for permanent force, $1,200,000; Edmonton, Royal Canadian Mounted Police barracks, $200,000; Kingston, Ontario Royal Military College, $350,000-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Do you object to that?

I am not objecting. I am pointing out that these military and police buildings are all being run in under the pretext of being in the nature of unemployment relief. They ought to be in the estimates either of national defence or of the public works department. Then again, a little further on: Montreal, Quebec, armoury, $200.000, and then: City of Ottawa, building to be put up here for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, site acquired, $1,200,000. Finally, Vancouver, armoury, $240,000. Here are large sums being voted in this measure for police and military purposes. I think that instead of spending a couple of million dollars for barracks and police buildings in the west at the present time as relief, it would be much better to spend the equivalent amount in constructing stock watering reservoirs which would be of service to the farmers of Alberta.
That is a provincial matter.

That is the kind of relief that would mean something to the people of the province. This business of always bringing forward some humane or alleged patriotic purpose to do in one way what the government hesitates to do in an entirely different way namely in the open, is the kind of thing in this bill that I object to above everything else.

I wish to make a suggestion to the Minister of Public Works. As i understand it he is moving an amendment that the amount of $1,200,000 for a barracks at Calgary be in Calgary or any other place in the province of Alberta. I would suggest
to him that there is $1,500,000 to be spent in the city of Toronto; why not move an amendment that that be spent, if not in Toronto, in some other parts of the province of Ontario.
If there was any specific reason we might do that.
I might be able tc point out some specific reason.
I think the minister is making a mistake in moving thal amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am moving it.

Or the Prime Minister. If it is going to cost $1,200,000 to construct a police barracks in Calgary, why not spend it and take the responsibility of spending it? This is one of the reasons why I object to the power taken by the government to transfer items.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no such power being taken.

We are
either voting these items as relief or as a straight estimate. I take it we are voting it as relief.
Relief would be the same.

As far as I am concerned, as a representative from the province of Alberta I have no particular objection to the expenditure in Banff. I hardly think that the Prime Minister should be charged with discrimination in that regard, because the park is a national institution for the benefit of all the people of Canada. But if these items are for relief, and as the city of Edmonton and the city of Calgary are almost equal in population, with an almost identical relief problem, why are we voting for the city of Calgary as a relief proposition -quite apart from whether it is East Calgary or West Calgary-in the neighbourhood of $1,400,000, and only $200,000 for the city of Edmonton? I have a protest from the mayor and council of that city about this matter, and I would not be doing my duty if I did not bring it to the attention of parliament. Edmonton's responsibility in the way of relief is just as great as that of Calgary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Yet I hear hon. gentlemen saying-and I am not protesting-that it is necessary for these works to be performed by local labour. That leaves Edmonton in a bad position, particularly as

the government have announced that they are not going to continue direct relief. Naturally the mayor and council of Edmonton are exercised over this matter. In the city of Calgary, with a population of about 80,000,
81.400.000	is to be spent, which is a vastly different proposition from the expenditure of
8200.000	in Edmonton, provided, as I have said, it is for relief, and that direct relief is to cease.
