speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I also had a letter from the mayor of Edmonton, and I wrote a letter to him. The reason that only 8200,000 is allotted there is that there was no other public work or undertaking required in Edmonton for which federal expenditure could be made. That was the position. In consequence of correspondence and negotiations with the provincial government we believe we have plans that will take care of the unemployment situation in the north. I quite agree with everything the hon. gentleman has said; I am fully aware of it. I wrote to the mayor, and I say to the hon. gentleman now, that public necessity was the reason for these items in the schedule, and not otherwise. In view of the fact that the capitol buildings have been constructed to the extent they have and the university buildings to the extent they have, and other public buildings such as the post office, there did not seem to be any building that was suggested by the construction survey or by our own except the barracks for the mounted police. The reason they were included was that it is better than paying rent. As there is no interest payable on the money used in the construction of these works, the whole $40,000,000 being available under the circumstances to which I alluded the other day, and as the amount we pay for rentals is very substantial, this will represent a great saving which will enure to the benefit of the taxpayers of Canada.

I would point out to the Prime Minister that there is a very considerable expenditure to be made in the national park at Jasper-I intend to refer to it when we come to it-and would ask that some special attention be given to drafting men from Edmonton for that work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so.
I want to say a word regarding this shifting of items from one place to another-
There is nothing of the kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman speaks of that I want to say that the barracks is not a question of shifting, but they have to go some place in the province of Alberta if the permanent unit is to remain in that province. That is the reason for that provision. .
Then I take it that the Prime Minister's position is that this building shall be built, but the site is not yet settled?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That might be.

If the site for that building is not settled I say leave this estimate until some definite site can be submitted to the committee. That is the way to pass public works estimates-know where you are going to place the building before putting the amount for it in the estimates. The members of this house should pass not only on the site but on the building and the amount.
Then I want to say something in regard to the buildings in Ontario. In Ontario-and it strikes me this is not complimentary to this government-large sums are to be spent in the ridings of certain members of the government. I refer particularly to the grants to the city of Guelph, the city of Fort William, and the city of Kingston-it also I think is large-having regard to other places for which this bill makes no provision at all. I was Minister of Public Works long enough to know that if you have the money you can find plenty of places to spend it to good advantage, but I do not think it is complimentary to the government itself to have these large sums going to the constituencies represented by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and1 the Minister of Railways and Canals. I am glad to see the Minister of Justice here; I happen to have before me his views on these buildings at a time when there was money in this country with which to construct them. May I be pardoned for a moment if I refer the house to Hansard of March 10, 1927, when we were passing estimates not for a few million but for a few thousand dollars. The present Minister of Justice was complaining about an item of some $12,000, and he said:
As I said before, if we had the money in the treasury, if our finances were in a flourishing condition, these buildings might be all

Public Works Construction
right; they might be very appropriate in these places. But these places have waited for a long time without any very great public inconvenience that we know about, and I say there is no warrant 'whatever for the expenditure of $20,000 at this place any more than there is for the expenditure of $12,000 at Kensington, Prince Edward Island.
Those were the days when we were reducing the debt and reducing taxation; we had money with which to construct buildings. I want to tell my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works that the people of this country, on whose backs this taxation will fall, are suffering about as badly this year as they have suffered in any year of their existence. That applies particularly to the farming communities, and I see that in this list of buildings those communities are overlooked to the greatest degree.
A couple of years ago the government told us, in regard to unemployment relief, that they would like to have suggestions from all members of the house. At that time I took the liberty of suggesting to the Minister of Labour that he relieve the rural constituencies, in which there were no harbours and which perhaps could get along for a few years longer without public (buildings, by eliminating as many as possible of the level crossings. I directed attention particularly at that time to the work that this would supply to men and teams in rural constituencies, many of which are not receiving a dollar of the money being expended by this government. Nothing of that kind has been done.

My hon. friend is mistaken. We passed special votes for the board of railway commissioners to assist them in eliminating railway crossings. I well remember at least $1,000,000 being voted for that purpose, so my hon. friend is not right in saying that nothing of that sort has been done.
In what year was that?
I direct my hon. friend's attention to the fact that these level crossings still exist.
There are thirty thousand of them in Canada.
And there are just about as many now as there were when hon. gentlemen opposite took office.
There are a few less.

Unfortunately, in the county in which I live, and in the adjoining county, there are a great many very dangerous railway crossings. A short time ago in the town of
Rodney we had a level crossing accident in which four or five of the flower of the Canadian nation were wiped out in a flash. This is happening every day; you cannot pick up a newspaper without reading of such accidents, yet we have these large amounts expended in urban districts with very little consideration given the rural districts. I very much object to that.
I notice that in this schedule there are amounts to be expended generally; I want to make a plea to the Minister of Public Works, and I hope he will pay attention while I make it. I do think that, out of the amount he will have at his disposal, he could very well utilize a substantial sum to assist the railways in eliminating level crossings. I say the same to the Minister of Railways with regard to the sum he will handle. The Minister of Public Works was good enough to supply me with the estimates for each department, and after all, while he talks about these not being public works in part, let me call his attention to the fact that of this total sum nearly $30,000,000 is for the Department of Public Works. There is $700,000 for the marine department, $15,000 for national defence, $2,000,000 for interior, $500,000 for Indian affairs and $240,000 for railways and canals. I do think that if you are going to attempt to give work to men and teams in the rural constituencies you cannot do it in any better way or in any way which will arouse less jealousy as between the different parts of the community than by endeavouring to eliminate these level crossings which are such a great menace to the people of this country.

In reading over this schedule I was very much surprised to find such a small grant for the province of Saskatchewan. If this were divided according to population the province of Saskatchewan should receive between $3,000,000 and $4,000,000, but we find only something like $675,000 going to that province. I do not think any part of the world or any part of the Dominion of Canada has suffered as much or needs employment more than Saskatchewan. A short time ago the Prime Minister said that he had in mind only two things in drawing up this schedule, first the relief of unemployment and second the necessity of the work. If he had those two things in mind I would suggest that there is no section of Canada that is more in need of aid than the southern part of Saskatchewan, and the southern part of western Canada generally. For five years these people have had no crops; for five years they have been practically on the dole. The neces-
Public Works Construction

sity for relief of some kind or other is appalling. If the condition existing in Saskatchewan to-day were to come about overnight, like the Halifax disaster some years ago, we would find relief coming from every section of the world, but here we do not find a dollar given to the people in that part of Saskatchewan to help them in any way.
One of two things must be done. Either those people in the southern part of Saskatchewan must be moved out and the land abandoned or something must be done in order to rehabilitate them. I suggest to the government that something should be done to rehabilitate these people on the land. I still have faith in that part of the country, remembering as I do that for twenty years, from 1909 to 1929, it produced an average of something like twenty bushels to the acre. Those people believe they can still produce crops if climatic and other conditions become favourable. To-day they are suffering from three things, first from climatic conditions, second from soil drifting and third from pests of different kinds which have to be combated. I wish to refer particularly to soil drifting. Not one thing has been done to enable these people to combat soil drifting. This condition is spreading from the south to the north, across the open prairies of Saskatchewan. I say this government should do something about it. Something should be done, and done immediately. Things should be taken in hand either by a commission or by a body of men familiar with conditions in the country. They should buy the necessary amount of seeds, such as broom grass, crested wheat grass, rye grass and things of that kind, and those [DOT]grasses should be supplied free of charge. The people should be taught how to use it and what to do in order to prevent soil drifting which is seriously affecting the prairies and destroying our lands.
This question is of paramount importance not only to the citizens of Saskatchewan, but to the whole of western Canada. If something of the kind is not done that section of western Canada will have to be abandoned and the people will have to be moved out. They have depended on one thing, and one thing only, to prevent soil drifting, and that is moisture. Moisture has come at certain times, and to a certain extent it has prevented the drift, but not to a sufficient degree to be effective.
This condition must be studied from a scientific standpoint. I would be out of order if I were to suggest or to move any vote for

these purposes. I have before me a newspaper clipping dealing with this subject.
Saskatchewan's master farmers, agricultural experts and departmental officials will meet in conference to discuss and seek solution for the soil drifting problem.
Hon. W. C. Buckle, Minister of Agriculture, in discussing the need for such a conference said:
"There seems to be too great reliance upon soil moisture conditions alone, to prevent soil drifting. It would appear to be necessary to give greater attention to strip farming and cover crops as tillage methods."
I suggest to the minister that something must be done. There is a grant in the schedule for a building in Regina. I do not know what building it is, but I will say this: Buildings are all right, but invariably when one building is erected another is emptied. That is the condition, unless there happens to be no building in existence. In using an old building the only consideration is the rent which must be paid, and if you are paying too much rent you must cut it down. Some of thiis money provided for in the schedule should be given to the farmers to buy seed, to build dams to preserve the moisture in order to prevent the soil drifting. I urge that the Minister of Public Works should take the matter up with the Minister of Agriculture, that something should be done at on-ce to teach these people what can be done to prevent the drift, and to bring back the conditions which obtained in the past. Knowing that a new grant cannot be made, I have seen fit to move, seconded by Mr. Bothwell:
That item No. 145 of schedule A be struck out and that the moneys therein provided be used for the purchase of grass and other seeds and for such other forms of state aid wdthin the limit of this vote as circumstances and conditions after thorough and competent inquiry may warrant in order to intelligently and systematically assist the farmers in the dried out areas of the west to rehabilitate themselves.

Mr. Chairman, it is not necessary to rule the amendment out of order. We are on a roving commission anyway; we are going here, there and all over Canada, in one province and another. We want something before us for a little while besides pork barrels, hogsheads and that sort of thing, do we not? This proposed expenditure of $40,000,000 launched a few days ago was especially to take care of the unemployed. It is now understood that it is for pork barrel purposes, about three-quarters of it. In his defence the Prime Minister mentioned nothing about unemployment. He tried to defend it on another score altogether.
We all remember the time the right hon. gentleman had in getting elected in 1921; indeed he failed to get elected at that time. His back is against the wall as badly to-day as it was in 1921. I hope the Liberals will not join with the Labourites in Calgary as they did in 1921; that would be too dear a price to pay for the defeat of the Prime Minister. But if they did do it, they could defeat him, and he would require this pork barrel and several like it to avoid defeat. That would apply not only in Calgary, but to all the ministers in other parts of Canada. They know what happened in the present temper of the people to their confreres in Saskatchewan. There is not a seed Tory left over in the Saskatchewan legislature for another campaign. They will have to get seed Tory relief through the peace, order and good government provisions passed by this aggregation over here, the so-called government of Canada. It is about time they were asking for another mandate, if I know anything. They are cutting up didos like this, trying to get a few seats by redistribution, trying to swipe a few more seats through the franchise bill, and hoping to retain power by those and other questionable means. And now the pork barrel is being rolled around into nearly every Tory constituency.
You had better get out of its way.
Who is trying to talk? Now the committee has a proposition. My right hon. leader-
He knows more about it than anybody else.
Order.
Are you calling me to order?
No.

I advise nobody to try that trick. I am not in the humour at all. I will bid good-bye to the government after prorogation, and express all kinds of good wishes and good will, but I will not wish them a return to power. I will have lots of good fellowship with them, but I am not in the humour to allow the prorogation of this house without protesting against these almost desperate and heroic efforts made by the government to retain power. That is exactly what they are doing all this session and did most of last. My right hon. leader suggests that instead of all these buildings on the prairies we might better consider the advisability of trying to put agriculture into something like permanently decent shape, especially in southern Saskatchewan and Alberta. I would ask any hon. member in this building to dare-
Oh, oh.

To dare, I say, to declare out of order or even challenge the appropriateness of this proposition. The hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) is making a practical proposition, and my right hon. leader did the same. What good would those cities be, anyway if there were no farmers around and about them? I want to risk any reputation I have by stating that much of southeastern Saskatchewan can be rehabilitated. I have studied them and lived on the plains for over fifty years. Not only have I studied the plains in Canada but, not personally but through interviews and reading I have studied the plains of Russia, and I know something about windy farming conditions.
What are my hon. friends grinning about over there?-empty heads that have no knowledge of prairie agriculture. I do not expect them to, nor have they had an opportunity to learn of it. I want to say right now that this government has been looking on complacently for the last four years as if everything was going well on those southwestern plains. And they have never raised one hand to avert the impending disaster rapidly approaching those formerly wonderfully fertile plains, converting those great productive lands into an Arabian or Sahara desert. That condition has come about by soil erosion and through the action of hurricane winds. The government has not done a thing-point to one, and I will apologize. I am going to mention one teeny, weeny, little bit the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) tried to do. He did get
Public Works Construction

some money to start the distribution of clover and grass seed. That might have helped but I have been able to find little if any of it in that vast southwest country. He just got this policy nicely started when his colleagues cut the Minister of Agriculture's estimates to the bone. Now they are putting up buildings and making all kinds of unnecessary expenditure ; they are spending forty millions under this bill, of which three-quarters is for election purposes, and leaving that great country destitute. No one is stretching out a hand to help it at this critical time. It must be either helped or abandoned.
Saskatchewan for its population has received more money from this government than any other province, and has received more help per capita than any other portion of Canada.
Why did they give a million and a half to Calgary and only $400,000 to Regina if Saskatchewan is hit worst?
Because we have given $30,000,000 to Saskatchewan already.
They are paying good interest on it.

The Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) is getting a good hunk himself. Outside of the little bit the Minister of Agriculture has provided as already mentioned, nothing has been done towards seeding down and rebuilding that area. It is just a fleabite, what has been done towards permanent cure-something you could put in your eye and not see any the worse for it. That is all that has been done to avert the calamity which has been facing that country since 1929.
The wind is driving the soil all over creation. The reports from Sault Ste. Marie stated that the sun was blinded this spring with the dust from the Saskatchewan and Alberta plains. They had to turn on their gaslights at midday to dispel the gloom occasioned by the prairie dust. Although the average farm may have a mortgage, even that will not hold down the soil if these high winds prevail. Our farms are being strewn anywhere between the Rocky mountains and the Great lakes, and even farther. This government have taken no responsibility in this matter. What steps have they taken? Not one, except the little mite of the Minister of Agriculture, and I do not think any of that found its way into that territory. My right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) has suggested
[Mr. Motherwell.!
that if water supplies were secured it would remedy one serious condition at least. The hon. member for Willow Bunch has suggested that something be could done in the way of giving assistance to the farmers in order to make it possible for them to rehabilitate themselves. They know how but they have not the wherewithal to carry out their know-how. They are down and out; they are out at the elbows and down at the heels. They cannot raise themselves and go under their own steam because they are too impoverished. They must receive state aid for permanent cures. As the hon. member for Willow Bunch has said, there are two alternatives. We must either abandon that vast territory or come to its aid and get it on its feet. You cannot go along the way you have been doing for the last five years with a policy of doles and feed and all that sort of thing, because you will have a charge on both the federal and the provincial authorities in perpetuity. They will never come back enough by themselves to make a new start.
What is to be done? There is only one way to stop drifting. I admire the heroics of my good friend Mr. Bryant who conceived the idea of planting enough carragana shrubs and hedges to stop the drifting. That gentleman was doing his best but I do not know how many years it would take to succeed via that route. I doubt if it could be done in one hundred years, and by that time we and our children will be dead. There is only one permanent way I know of to stop this soil drifting. Take the land held in the hands of the crown and seed it down with broom grass or some other suitable grass. Crested wheat may be used, but I think the broom is better. We should put that wind swept region back in the state in which we found it fifty years ago, restore it to its soddy condition. That would provide a binder to stop the drifting. The other fifty per cent of the land could be taken care of on a rotation basis, including fall rye grass ind clover. There will have to be some sind of a follow up policy, something like a land utilization commission to take charge of this vast area. There would have to be government supervision, there is no question about that. I remember when I had the privilege of being in the Regina house we had district representatives in that stricken area. Doctor Booth at the head of the economics branch was one of them. We knew there were special troubles which required special aids in order to enable the farmer to handle that country to advantage. But there is not one of these things being done.

Why? This government does not know enough about prairie agriculture to evolve a policy. How could they know? You cannot teach what you do not know yourself.
Is it not a fact that you brought in professors from the United States to try to seed that land and it proved an utter failure?

I cannot hear my hon. friend. I am used to the practice of talking just loud enough for Hansard to hear. Shout it out! Here, I will get my periscope on you. I have all the juice turned cun; get up, throw back your shoulders and let me hear you. Has the hon. member nothing to say? Then let him forever hold his peace and not be interrupting me.
This is a very serious matter. I have been a resident of Canada all my life and I have lived fifty-three years in my adopted province of Saskatchewan. What has happened in that vast southwest territory, during the past thirty years? They have grown wheat continuously till the fibre is gone in the windiest part of the west. That country is especially windy right up to the foothills. In hot weather the high winds create a peculiar suction upwards. This is only beginning to be understood. The soil is taken up in fine dust like flour. With another five years like the past, the top five or six inches of soil will be practically all gone-where to, I do not know. It will be in the gullies and sloughs; it can spread it over a thousand miles and yet show very thin. If the top soil is blown off for another five years, ninety per cent of the farmers in that area will be lying on their backs on the hard pan with their tummies and their toes turned up. That is what will happen. I see an hon. gentleman shaking his head as though I was trying to string him, but let me tell him that this is all true and all too true.
I was brought up on a farm in Ontario where the top-soil in one field was removed by fire in the clearing of it. This happened over a hundred years ago but it has never been the same since, although it has been fertilized with ashes, with strawy manure, buckwheat ploughed in, and so on. It is still just blue clay, as hard as a brick. It is bad enough when the top-soil is burned off, and the ashes are left behind, but when the topsoil is blown off nothing is left but the pebbles, which will not blow, and hardpan. That is an infinitely worse condition, and a hundred years of reclamation will not bring it back once you lose the top five or six inches of soil. I cannot see how hon. gentlemen can defend their non-action in endeavoring to meet this 74726-289
condition. This area is one of the most productive parts of the prairies; if it gets seven or eight inches of rain or even less during the growing season it will then produce magnificent crops of thirty or forty bushels to the acre-I have seen crops of fifty or sixty bushels -of the highest quality wheat on what is now a bleak wilderness. If this great period of production had been distributed over the whole period since that country was first settled about thirty years ago, it would average a very nice crop every year, of about fifteen or eighteen bushels to the acre. The farmers thus far have been producing therefore an average of fifteen to eighteen bushels to the acre. But it seems that our predisposition is to plunge, to let money burn a hole in our pocket unless it is spent, expanding and expanding. And can you blame them, having obtained these magnificent crops and being innoculated with the virus of empire farming, undertaking vast areas run by combine and power farming generally. In other words, they invested their money in larger operation. That used to be the right thing to do, the enterprising thing, but it is not setting aside anything for a rainy day or making the fat years carry the lean. We all admit that we have made mistakes, and the more unusually prosperous one is in good times the more likely one will be left on his haunches when the hard time comes due to the policy of excessive exhaustion. I don't know whether this is getting into the craniums of hon. gentlemen opposite, or not, but there are not so many of them just now giving me that senseless grin that characterized them at the beginning of this talk. I am not talking for fun's sake but to point out a danger that hangs over a fine piece of our country which in ordinary years can carry itself. But the people there have had five bad years and this is the sixth, and they can carry on no longer without confronting the whole state with the problem as to whether they will vacate that country en masse with the aid of the government or start in now with something else than putting up city buildings which we have done without all along. The one in Calgary may be quite warranted and the Prime Minister may need it to get elected. And I should like to see him elected, because I do not like to see another shut-out such as there was in Saskatchewan recently ; I should like to see at least one hon. gentleman on the opposite side returned at the coming election. So that if they can succeed in getting one elected by putting in another million in Calgary, go to it. But I say, do something for the rehabilitation of agriculture without which that country,

I wish to take a few minutes of the time of the committee to discuss the program now under review. It will probably to some extent take care of unemployment throughout Canada in our cities and towns but so far as a certain portion of western Canada is concerned, which the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) and the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) have brought to the attention of the committee to-night, a situation exists on account of which the people need work just as badly as do the people in the cities and towns. This is a problem that the federal government will have to solve sooner or later because I hold the federal government responsible very largely for conditions that now exist since they invited people to settle in a part of the country that should never have been settled. I do not apply that to the whole of Saskatchewan; southern Saskatchewan has been an extraordinarily fertile portion of the west, but because of certain conditions, more particularly because of

the lack or the running out of fibre in the soil, the situation has altered very much from that in the earlier days when the soil there was more productive. But as regards the constituency I represent and a very substantial portion of the country straight south from where I live to the international boundary, I know when it was proposed to open up that territory and to invite settlement there, the officers of the department, and in fact the minister who was responsible for opening it up-and it was a Liberal minister who did this-were warned against opening up that part of the dominion.
What happened was this: a tremendous settlement grew up and people took money in there; they spent their time and labour and to-day thousands of them have been forced out of that area with very little thanks from the people of Canada for their efforts in trying to settle up that territory and make it productive. I still hold that the federal government is responsible for that condition and because of that fact I expect the federal government to take some steps to relieve it. When I communicated with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) in regard to certain projects that might be undertaken as relief measures, he pointed out to me very emphatically that the proposals which I had made came under the authority of the provincial government. That is quite true; I admit it. Nevertheless, because of the responsibility of the federal government for opening up that part of the country and because of the need of the people to secure some money with which to buy food, even though they have farms there, I maintain that something should be done and done very soon in those districts.
I remember in 1922 and 1923 we were considering the possibility of rehabilitating that portion of the country because of a couple of dry years. I recall that I suggested to the then Minister of Agriculture, now the hon. member for Melville, certain things which might be done to relieve that situation. For instance I suggested the damming up of all the coulees and the low places for the purpose of holding water for stock. I suggested also the planting of trees along the road allowances and so forth, and also providing for seed for the reseeding of grass in order to put fibre back in the soil. I suggested to the then Minister of Agriculture that I did not expect the farmers to get paid fully for the work they were doing. I suggested that the federal government, in view of the responsibility it had for opening up that part of the country for settlement, might give some slight assistance merely to induce the farmers

Public Works Construction
to do these things which eventually, in my judgment, would assist that area very substantially. The then Minister of Agriculture refused to take any steps or to do anything to save the situation. True, it was not as bad then as it is now and it did not extend to Saskatchewan, but now that he finds the same condition has extended to that province, he begins to think it is necessary to do something to help his people. But I am sure if we had started at that particular time a policy of tree planting, not in small groves around the farms of the people but along the road allowances for miles and miles in order to break the hot winds of that country, and also of damming up all the surplus water that runs off from the melting of the snow in order to create more humidity in that area, I am sure we would not have the condition that we have to-day, but the then Minister of Agriculture did not see fit to do anything in that regard.
I remember that the then leader of the Conservative party, now leader of the Senate, supported me in my viewpoint. I merely take the time now to impress upon the government the necessity of giving some consideration to the problem. I can assure the government that so far as the people on those farms are concerned, they are to-day just as hard up for food as are many people in the cities, true they have some live stock but they have nothing to feed them. While it might be expected that they would be able to produce a very substantial portion of their food supplies, yet when one has had experience of that part of the country and seen how their gardens and everything they have put in after great labour and expense in providing the seed, shrivel and dry up and they get nothing for their labour, one understands the troubles they have and the necessity of giving some consideration to the problem. I therefore suggest to the government that they take any steps they deem necessary to consult with the government not only of Alberta but of Saskatchewan in order to see if something can be done as soon as possible to relieve the situation.

I had not intended to say anything at this time because it seems so absolutely hopeless in the dying hours of parliament that any plea we could make would induce the government to alter its policy. In this schedule there are special items for various classes of public buildings and we are told that they are necessary and that that is the reason they are selected. I would say that the fundamental purpose of these works is to distribute purchasing power
among the people, to give work in order that those employed may through their work get money and thus find relief. If we are to have $40,000,000 distributed among the people, there are better ways of spending this amount than by erecting these public buildings. It seems to me that we are thinking altogether too much in the terms of public buildings. I know in the past that is the way in which the Dominion government has spent its money; I know that is the accepted way, but we have reached a stage when that is not the best way of spending this amount. There are other ways that would distribute this $40,000,000 among the people and at the same time would serve the country better than it would be served by the erection of a large number of public buildings. Of course I am very glad that in my own city we shall have one more federal building added, but I would infinitely rather have the government do something to supply the housing needs of the people of Winnipeg. This would mean the same expenditure of money on the part of the dominion government, the same amount of money coming into the pockets of the carpenters, masons and so forth but we would have something that would be of immediate and very substantial service to the people of Winnipeg. Someone may say immediately: That is a municipal or a provincial matter and the federal government cannot do that kind of thing. Why can they not? The municipality or the province would be only too glad if they did. The administrative detail can be worked out. If necessary a corporation might be constituted that would rent the houses In the meantime there are thousands of people in my own city of Winnipeg who are ill housed. A federal building, however beautiful, will not take the place of houses that these people ought to have.
As to this building under discussion, a barracks, it may be necessary-the Prime Minister seems to think it is-that the soldiers should be permanently housed, but I submit that there are many other things that should be done before that. This question of subway or overhead railway crossings, by which lives could be saved, is immensely more important. I do not see how we can do other than make this criticism of each item as it comes along, because only in this way can we point out the need for some other type of relief program.
Now I come to the matter mentioned bj the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr Donnelly). I was very glad that he had, shah I say the courage, to bring it up to-night. I
believe the members of this house are not
Public Works Construction

sufficiently seized of the seriousness of the problem in southern Saskatchewan, in parts of southern Alberta and of southern Manitoba. I overheard some hon. gentleman across the way say we should deal with this problem by ignoring it. Surely that shows lamentable ignorance of the urgency of the problem. There are two things that have to be dealt with, one the transfer of hundreds of thousands of our people within the next few months to an altogether different part of the country. Anyone who has seen these poor people trekking north with their goods loaded on their hayracks, not knowing where they are going and not finding enough grass along the way to keep their stock alive, must realize that it is a desperate condition. Our railways ought to be used, money ought to be advanced to enable them to build homes in the north, to break up land quickly enough that within the next year or two they would have some sort of return for their labour. The actual migration is taking place, but in my judgment there Should be a migration of thousands, perhaps tens of thousands of families, from those stricken districts. It is something on which we shall have to spend millions of dollars if an enormous amount of human suffering is to fbe prevented. Then we have the other problem; these large areas of our country in some way ought to be saved; if they are not, the destruction will be extended in every direction, because that soil drifting will not be restricted witlhin the area to which it is now limited but will grow worse. Again I do not think the eastern members realize the difficulty. I saw, within the last few weeks, alongside the railways, fences erected to keep the railway tracks from being covered by the drift, with sand piled against them four or five feet high. I remember years ago visiting Egypt and seeing where fences had been erected in the Roman days in an attempt to keep the sands back from the pyramids, and beyond them other fences erected by more recent engineers. That is precisely the kind of thing that is taking place in Saskatchewan. We are going to have to face it in a very serious form if prompt action is not taken. It seems to me that this government, instead of thinking as governments have always thought so much in terms of public buildings, ought rather to think in terms of the practical problems that confront us here and now. I would earnestly plead with the Prime Minister. He knows something of the west. I have been in the west since I was a child; I went there in 1882. over fifty years ago, and I know western problems, but I never saw conditions such as they are to-day. Housing conditions are bad enough

in many of our cities, and I would plead with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works that even yet they alter their method of providing this relief. I am very glad that they have found the forty million dollars. I am glad that they have come to the point where instead of giving direct relief they are providing works by which people can earn a certain amount of money and for which there will be something to show. All that is to the good. But I submit there are particular types of work that can be done to much greater advantage than the public buildings proposed. I would urge that even at this late stage the government give serious consideration to a complete revision of this program.

The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) left the impression upon me that he was saying that somehow or other I preached in opposition something different from what I practised when we were in power. Anyone who thinks that is so has a chance to get up and say so. I say to the hon. member for Acadia in the kindest way I can that I wish he would particularize as to what that was. My then department had not charge of water supply. If anything like that was done, the minister of the interior, or public works, who was a resident of Alberta, did have charge of certain lands, looked after certain weeds; his predecessor drained certain sloughs and he perhaps carried that on a little; certain activities of that nature came under the Department of the Interior. The Indians were, under that same department, and sometimes roads were constructed and that sort of thing. But I cannot think of anything that came under the purview of the Department of Agriculture that Saskatchewan got and Alberta did not get. There is one exception; that is there were no restricted areas established in Alberta to clean up bovine tuberculosis. Alberta was the only province in which they were not established, and my hon. friend knows why perfectly well. Alberta did not want it. He would be the last to say it should be imposed on them. I think the present Minister of Agriculture would be delighted, as soon as they are ready for a restricted area to be established in Alberta, to give them the same treatment the other provinces got in that respect. I would have been the most tickled man in the government if Alberta could have seen its

way to put itself in line with the rest of the dominion in that matter. But they had a perfect right to take the position they did; they were taken up with another method which might prove to have something in it, one that is developing all the time-the B.C.G. test, they call it. Some day they may find an immunizing serum to prevent tuberculosis instead of merely slaughtering the cattle that are found to have it. Science may accomplish that. Meantime until something better is found we were using the other tuberculin method.
When it was decided to establish a seed elevator in Saskatchewan, there was a good deal of dissatisfaction, and I got the consent of my leader to establish a similar institution, or something to correspond to it in Alberta and Manitoba. Because Alberta and Saskatchewan were twin sisters, bom at practically the same time, I was particularly anxious to treat them both evenly and justly. If I overlooked anything or departed in the least from that principle I would have taken it as a great favour if my hon. friend from Acadia had pointed it out to me when I was in a position to deal with it. I recall further that in order to aid in rehabilitating these great plains in the matter of grazing, while the interior department adjusted the regulations to the advantage of the ranchers on more occasions than one, the Department of Agriculture started a demonstration station at Manyberries in southern Alberta for the purpose of trying to rebuild the pastures of that one time great range country. They have been working on that for I suppose twelve years, to see what can be done to improve the pasture land for which that country was once so famous, not only for growing grass but growing high quality nutritious grass.
I think my hon. friend knows about that. However, if he is in the humour I am in, if he can find something that I neglected at that time I will have no hesitation in admitting it, but as my hon. friend says the situation then was not so serious as it is now. That is a big admission. No one ever dreamed that we would see these days. Even in what we called good times there was hard sledding in certain parts of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, but these difficult times came with the advent of the Tories, and I hope they will go away when the Tories go out of power. That is just by the way; it just happened that way. Other years will come, possibly with better crops and prices. This year it looks as though the world crop would be about five hundred million bushels less than last year, so it would seem that
nature is solving the problem of carry-overs much better than the international wheat agreements are.
Oh, oh.

I expected that from some yahoo over there in the rearguard. Well, it will soon be eleven o'clock, and we are not going to prorogue to-night. I believe in doing things decently and in order not by jamming them though in this way, proroguing in the dark midnight hours as though their deeds were evil.
I was devoting some attention to the well meant remarks of the hon. member for Acadia, which I think left a wrong impression as far as the Department of Agriculture was concerned. I have always found that hon. gentleman a pretty decent hon. gentleman, and I do not think he wants to misrepresent the situation. If he can point to any disparity between my attitude to-day and my attitude then, having regard to the different climatic and economic conditions, I am willing to be exposed. I do not want to take the ground that I am always right; time may prove that I have been wrong in some things this session. I do not think it will; I think time will prove that the stand I have taken this session was the right stand, but I will not feel humiliated if my hon. friend can point to something we failed to do in those days when we had the power to do it, but which we are preaching now. I will excuse hon. gentlemen on the opposite side for a moment if the hon. member for Acadia has anything further to add in that respect. I do not say that defiantly; I mean it in a kindly way.

I could not very well allow the hon. member for Melville to make the statement he has made without replying. He has suggested, together with the hon. member for Willow Bunch, certain things that should be done to rehabilitate the southern portion of Saskatchewan and parts of Alberta. I made the very same suggestions in 1923, not only personally to the Minister of Agriculture but also on the floor of this house. I suggested a policy which the government of that day might pursue in order to rehabilitate small areas then suffering from conditions similar to those existing to-day. The government of that day did not take any steps to remedy the situation, and I must say that if we had taken steps then along the lines suggested to-night we would have had some experience that could have been applied to the larger area where those conditions prevail at the present time.

I am sorry, but my right hon. leader was trying to get something into my head, and I could not listen to the hon. gentleman at the same time. Would he mind mentioning in a word what that specific matter was?

It is only necessary to mention these points: the re-seeding of large areas with grass, with assistance from the government to buy the seed; the damming up of the surplus waters in the spring in order to create humidity in those areas, and the planting of rows of trees up and down the road allowances in large areas in order to protect the land so that the dry winds would not blow the farm from one place to another. Those were the three suggestions I made in 1922 and again in 1923, but the government of the day could not see its way clear to accept my suggestion and give some financial aid in that regard.
The Department of Agriculture would have been responsible for only one item; that is grass and clover seed. I may explain that every experimental farm-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: STATEMENT OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION CONCERNING WANT OF CONFIDENCE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as no doubt hon. members are aware, it had been my intention on the motion for supply to move an amendment to the effect that the present administration no longer enjoys the confidence of the country. I think it is perfectly obvious that such is the case. May I say, however, that I realize all hon. members of the house are very anxious, if at all possible, to conclude this week. I understand if we do not conclude to-night by midnight or before midnight, that we will have to adjourn until Tuesday, as to-morrow is Sunday and Monday is Dominion day, and there being reasons which make it impossible to conclude the work of the session on Monday.
In these circumstances I feel I should be embarrassing the house unnecessarily if I proceeded with the motion to-night which I intended should be the last motion of what 1 believe and hope will be the last session of this parliament. Should I be mistaken, and should there be another, namely a sixth session of this parliament, I shall, if circumstances permit, make it the first motion of that new session. Meantime I think there will be further evidence, both through byelections and probably further provincial elections, that the government no longer enjoys the confidence of the people. I do sincerely feel that this administration has lost completely the confidence of the country, and that it should no longer continue in office. The Prime Minister might well advise us that this being the end of the fifth session of this Parliament, the session will be followed by dissolution. The supply we are voting will be needed in large part to carry on the work of the government through the remainder of the present fiscal year, that is until March 31, 1935. I do not wish to embarrass the government in its effort to obtain what is needed
of that supply. If however parliament should not be dissolved and this government should come back and ask the house to vote supply for the year ending March 31, 1936, I wish to say that the opposition will do all in its power to prevent this government obtaining any further supply.

I wish to say one word at this time. I had intended to make some extended observations with respect to the tariff board, but under the present circumstances I shall curtail my remarks. In bringing down the bill with regard to the tariff board two years ago the Prime Minister made it abundantly clear, as reported in Hansard at page 3422, that this was to be a court of record. He said:
We are creating a court of record with all that appertains and belongs to a court of record.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That was Part I, and the hon. gentleman knows it. It has nothing to do with Part II.
My right hon. friend says that was Part I.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: You have made misrepresentations long enough; if we sit here until Tuesday I shall not let those remarks pass.

I do not know what the
right hon. gentleman means when he states it was Part I. He provided that it was to be a court of record for all purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is not so.

He made provision whereby it was to have a seal, it was to have the power of summoning witnesses, and was to have all the perquisites of a court of record. But what did the Supreme Court of Canada say? In the judgment of the court I find this:
The board of customs was, and the tariff board is, in no sense, a court. By force of the provisions of the Customs Act, it is not a judicial body but an administrative body. Its functions were and are purely departmental.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is what we always said.

That is the court which my right hon. friend always described as a court of record. He told us he was getting a gentleman of the highest judicial qualifications to preside over it. He felt that a court should be appointed for the purposes outlined in his speech on the imperial conference agreement, at page 114 of Hansard, 1932. This is what he said at that time:
We have therefore provided that our tariff board shall act as a judicial body as well as a fact finding body, in so far as their functions of interpreting the agreement are concerned.
That statement is to be found in Hansard of October 12, 1932, at page 114, When the board made a decision with which the government did not agree, instead of my right hon. friend referring to the supreme court the question whether or not the board had made a correct decision, he was careful to make no such reference at all. Instead of that, he referred to the supreme court the question whether the board had jurisdiction. The supreme court expressly refrained from deciding whether the tariff board were right or wrong in their decision.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It certainly did.
My right hon. friend says it certainly did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Decided it had no jurisdiction.

But it did not decide
whether or not the tariff board were right or wrong in the accuracy of the decisions they made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They could not have been right.
Let me read to my right hon. friend what they said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I know it.

I read from the judgment of the court:

Copies of the decisions of the board upon the concrete eases mentioned in the order in council, and' also of the reasons for judgment in one of these cases were submitted to the court; but they were placed before us only for the purpose of illustration; and by the questions put, the court is not asked to say if these decisions were right or wrong. It was made clear at the argument that in our answers we are to limit ourselves to the abstract questions referred to us.
The abstract question was not:	Was the
tariff board right or wrong? it was: Has the tariff board jurisdiction? In submitting that case to the supreme court as he did, it seems to me that my right hon. friend intended to discredit the tariff board before the people of this country and the old country. He submitted a question which attacked only its jurisdiction but he deliberately left unchallenged the question as to whether its decision was right or wrong.
I am not going to develop this matter any further although there is a great deal more which could be said. The thing my right hon. friend should have done instead of referring these abstract questions to the supreme court was to make it positive by legislation that the tariff board was intended to carry out the functions which everyone thought it was intended to carry out under Part II of the act. What was the use of saying, as my right hon. friend did, that the tariff board was to be free from political considerations when as a matter of fact it has to go with its hat in its hand and ask the Minister of National Revenue to approve of the decisions which it makes. The right hon. gentleman stated in parliament that it was intended to substitute an independent tribunal for a political tribunal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He was dealing with
Part I.

The right hon. gentleman continued:
You have in the one instance a political body, governed by all the considerations that influence political bodies; and we all know just what the pressure of contending interests may be to get a minister to make a recommendation to council. As against that we have this body which is not interested in political matters and makes its decisions free from political influence.
My right hon. friend says he was referring to Part I. Does he mean to suggest that it was to be a political body as far as Part II was concerned? Surely not. My right hon. friend left the impression upon our friends from over the seas, and he left the impression upon this house, that this was to be a board having judicial functions.

Supply-National Revenue

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And it has in connection with Part I; the people overseas were not interested in Part II.

Part I simply gives the
power to find facts and suggest to the government what changes might be made in the tariff, and how much tariff should be levied in order to equalize the costs of production. It has no judicial functions in the sense of making a decision which is binding upon anyone. Under Part II it had appeals from the dominion appraiser, and it was expected that it would have some judicial function. What is the use of taking an appeal from the dominion appraiser and solemnly going to this tariff board which has all the paraphernalia of a court, and then after the tariff board has made a decision, coming back to the Minister of National Revenue and asking him if he will please approve the decision of the tariff board? Who will ever go to the tariff board to have that judicial function exercised under Part II when as a matter of fact he would have to go back to the minister to have the decision approved? I do not think my right hon. friend believed that under section 48 the tariff board would have to come back to the Minister of National Revenue to obtain approval of their decision. If he did believe that, then I think he misled the house and the country when he laid down what the functions of the tariff board were to be and when he described the qualifications necessary for the personnel of that board. I say to my right hon. friend that the country was disappointed when he announced in this house that he was not going to legislate to give the tariff board the status to which it is entitled and which it has attained before the people of this country.
I shall take up but a minute more of the time of the house to quote an extract from the Financial Post of June 23, which expresses much better than I can the feeling of this country.

Is my right hon. friend going to say that he is afraid to have read in
this house a short statement by a reputable journal which does not reflect upon any member of this house?

My right hon. friend has made that statement a number of times but he will find no such rule about introducing another member. The rule he will find is the one which states that you cannot read anything which reflects on the proceedings of the house.

Amount required to carry out agreement between His Majesty and the municipality of the village of St. Vincent de Paul for extension of the present water and sewer system connected with St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, $3,000.

I had the floor when this item was up before. I am going to detain the committee only a few minutes. I am compelled to speak to-night on behalf of those guards who were dismissed by the new administration some years ago to promote efficiency. Their notice to go was in these terms: "Guard So and So: Acting under instructions from Ottawa, I have to advise that you will be retired from the staff of this institution to promote efficiency;" or: "Guard So and So: Acting on instructions from Ottawa, I have to advise that you have been retired from your position on the staff of this institution, to take effect from the 25th, to promote efficiency." I have a dozen of them here, notices to men who were dismissed by this new administration to promote efficiency, and now we have information that for eighteen months there has been no efficiency, though these gentlemen have lost their positions. I want to say on behalf of these guards that, at the time the riots occurred, the new superintendent came to my door, without solicitation from myself after he had dismissed about five or six of them, and gave me the promise that these men would be restored. He gave me a straight promise that they would be restored. I went to these men and begged them not to raise any disturbance but to keep quiet because they would be put back in their positions, and I told them that on the word of the superintendent. That word was not fulfilled, but instead of that about thirty more were dismissed. I am speaking to-night on behalf of these men, pointing out the injustice that has been done them. In addition to that, I would point out that if Warden Megloughlin has been dismissed, the people want to know on what ground and for what reasons. Was he dismissed because he was inefficient? Was he dismissed because he had not support from higher up? Or was it because he was carrying out some administration of his own or the administration laid down for him? These are matters that are disturbing to the people of Kingston and to the

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
guards who have been dismissed.. It is too late to discuss the matter to-night, but I can assure the committee that, having waited patiently for some time for an explanation of their dismissal, I am speaking now only in the interests of the penitentiary. No matter what any newspaper or anyone may say, I am expressing my own views, and I have at heart the welfare of these guards and of the people of Kingston as well as of the penitentiary. The people of Kingston are disturbed after the disclosure that has been made to the house that efficiency has not been secured, although a dozen or two of guards have been dismissed. I have done my duty, and though I have not time to-night to discuss the matter further I promise you that I shall return to the subject at the very beginning of the next session of parliament.

Unfortunately it always happens that the penitentiary estimates come up at the very close of the session. I have sat through this session and listened to a good deal of good talk and a good deal that might have been better left unsaid, and I intend to-night to take up as much time as I would two weeks before prorogation.
In the winter the Minister of Justice, discussing the Kingston penitentiary riots, said that they were due to communist activities in that institution. When General Ormond, who was superintendent of penitentiaries in Canada, was listing the causes of the riots in Canada he enumerated eleven, and the last one was the only cause that could be interpreted as communistic. Oddly enough, the riot of October 17-20, 1932, was by no means the only one in Kingston. I take my information from Superintendent Ormond's reports. There was an uprising in Kingston on September 17, 1921; another on January 17, 1923; another on October 3, 1924; another on January 22, 1927, and some sort of disturbance called the conspiracy on August 5, 1931. Then there were the riots in October, 1932. It would be interesting to bear from the Minister of Justice what caused all the other riots, since many of them took place before the communists were in Kingston. It is too thin a reason to give to an intelligent body like the House of Commons, and I think that the events since that speech was made by the Minister of Justice have borne out the contention that the reason simply was not good enough. The minister at that time took the ground that the 50,000 communications he had received asking for an investigation into our penal institutions were from communist sources. I do not know where they came
from, but I do know that the Toronto Globe, which could not by any stretch of imagination be said to be a communist journal, for weeks and even months campaigned in favour of an impartial investigation into the difficulties at Kingston. And not only the Globe, but other newspapers, such a journal as the Whig Standard of Kingston and more recently, since the debate in the House of Commons a few days ago, the Hamilton Herald and many others, have asked for an impartial investigation into all Canadian penitentiaries and particularly Kingston penitentiary, where there has been one disturbance after another. Moreover, such eminent authorities as Archdeacon Scott and Mr. W. M. Nickle, K.C., of Kingston, who had much to do with the defence of certain convicts in Kingston and has for a long time been deeply interested in the conditions in the penitentiary, and whose father was one of three people who made the finest report on penitentiaries we have ever had, have urged such an investigation.
Possibly at this point I might say to the hon. member for Marquette that Major W. M. Nickle, in an interview given the Toronto Globe on Wednesday, June 27, made reference to the hon. gentleman in these terms:
Just to bring this matter to a head, I challenge Mr. Mullins to prove that any instance in my letter to Canon Scott is incorrect or false; and if the government will give me a chance I will prove that what I have stated in my letter is correct in every detail.
His letter, which was read on the floor by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, is a terrible indictment of the management of Kingston penitentiary. Surely there should not be required any further urging of the government for an impartial investigation. There should be a royal commission or a special committee of investigation to look into conditions not only in Kingston penitentiary but in all the penitentiaries throughout Canada.
I should like to take some time to give what I think are some of the causes of the riots.
I am going to quote for a moment or two from the decision of Judge Deroche in the Rex versus Kirkland case in which he says:
The men (meaning the inmates) had for months and possibly years been asking for the removal of certain grievances which were in their minds, with little or no response.
Then he goes on to say:
They now decided that on October 17, at three o'clock p.m. they would walk out of the shops and make a peaceful demonstration to impress the warden and through him Ottawa.

At the end of the judgment he says again on page 7:
Then to go back to the cause of the riot. This peaceful demonstration which developed into a riot, was for the purpose of emphasizing the demands of the men for redress of certain grievances which had been long and repeatedly denied them. Many of the grievances for which this demonstration was staged have already-
Before this trial took place.
-been granted to the men, proving conclusively to my mind that those demands must have been reasonable.
Those are the words of the judge who tried one of the rioters and in his opinion there was cause-not that the judge wanted a riot- and he gives as proof of his belief that the grievances which' the men enumerated were remedied between the time of the rioting and the judgment made by him. I am, however, inclined to think there has been a slipping backward between that day and this.
Then, too, I want to say something about the number of repeaters. The figures were given the other day by the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Ross), that in Canadian penal institutions twenty-one per cent of all the inmates are serving a term for their second offence; fourteen per cent for their third offence and twenty-two per cent for their fourth offence or over. Using a statement from Superintendent Ormond's report, seventy-five per cent of all the prisoners in Canadian penitentiaries have had previous convictions, for incarceration possibly not in penitentiaries, but, if not, at least in some other place such as a gaol or a reformatory. I remember one time Brigadier General Hughes told me that the average cost of a conviction was SI,200, so if we figure it out on that basis, the repeaters, using the percentage I have just given and the prison population of this year, mean an increased cost to the people of Canada of $6,735,600; that is the repeater cases over and above the first conviction. Therefore, I should think if the House of Commons is not affected by a humanitarian appeal it ought to be affected by a financial or purely material appeal. It is bad business to go on putting men into penitentiaries where they are not reformed, where apparently, after leaving such institutions, they cannot make a place for themselves in life and so return to prison.
I feel the House of Commons ought to take much more interest in this subject than hon. members have shown. It always happens just as it is happening now that this matter comes up at the very end of a session, one gets an indifferent house and nothing is done from year to year. So we have such cases as the

one mentioned in Mr. Nickle's letter and corroborated in Judge Deroche's statement that a man called O'Brien has been in solitary confinement in Kingston penitentiary from August, 1931, at least until July 12, 1933, and is quite probably still in solitary confinement. Since, however, the department guards its secrets so very carefully I cannot say whether that is still the case, but it is quite true that he was in solitary confinement for the period mentioned. Just think of it! a man in solitary confinement from August, 1931, to July 12, 1933! It would have been much more humane to stand him up against the wall and shoot him. The idea of putting a man into solitary confinement for a period running on into two years in a cell three or four times the size of a piano box, to use the term of the report prepared by Nielde, Biggar and Draper, and leaving him there for that length of time, although during that time he has never been tried for the offence for which he was committed to the solitary cell. Whether this has been done recently, I am not prepared to say I would like the Minister of Justice, when he replies, if he does reply, to tell us whether or not O'Brien is still in solitary confinement.
I have also been interested in the case of Tim Buck. There are various reasons for my interest in him. The committee will recall that it was said he was shot at. That was denied, but it was admitted the other day by the Minister of Justice that eleven shots were fired into the cell of Tim Buck. I notice that Major Nickle in an interview which he gave to the Toronto Globe recalled to us all that when crown counsel MacKay was questioning Tim Buck, he, Buck, stated that his cell was the only one of seventy-six cells in D range which was fired at. It would be interesting to me to know on what date he was fired at, whether it was on the riot of the seventeenth or the riot of the twentieth, and whether he was fired at from the corridor directly into the cell or whether he was fired at from the yard outside. It seems rather remarkable that if there are seventy-six cells in range D, one cell should be chosen and eleven shots should be fired into it. We were told the other day that they were fired into it in order to quiet or frighten Tim Buck. I should think it ought to have been a successful method. I do not know whether others in the house feel as I do about the matter, but to me it seems a remarkable action that one cell should have been chosen and these volleys should have been fired into it. The shots were all supposed to have lodged in the ceiling and it is very lucky for Buck that they did. If they were fired from

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
the yard outside they must have been fired by excellent marksmen if they hit the ceiling every time and did not hit Tim Buck.
I am going to quote Judge Deroche again. It was said by the minister that Buck was standing in the door of his cell encouraging the rioters. In this reiport the judge says on page 7:
Buck told them-
That is the .prisoners.
-that the soldiers would not hurt them if they did no violence to person or injury to property.
That does not sound very much like encouraging the rioters or like a terrifically dangerous man who needed to be fired at eleven times in order to cow him. I am going to quote again from page 3 of the same report; it is very much in the same language:
When it was announced that the soldiers were coming, one of the men, Tim Buck, advised the men that the soldiers could not or would not hurt them so long as they did no damage to property or violence to anyone, and instructed the men to gather pails of water and barricade the door, expecting to stand siege.
At the end of this document when Judge Deroche is giving judgment on Kirkland, he gives a modified judgment because he says that they did no injury to anyone. All that would lead one to think that there was possibly as much violence on the part of the authorities as there was on the part of the men.
There is one other protest I wish to make; I feel it is useless and still I want to make it.
I think we have altogether too much military control in penitentiaries. We started off with General Ormond, and then we had Colonel Megloughlin who now has been asked for his resignation. I want to point out that the technique which serves well with normal and healthy men and men more or less free, as soldiers are, would be quite different from the technique required for men who are morally or mentally sick, who are not free and who are embittered and therefore very difficult to deal with. I do not think that the method which works in one case will work in the other. We need to start as soon as possible to handle intelligently our prison population. We need a psychiatrist, as mentioned by General Ross, and we need segregation of prisoners. Possibly the Minister of Justice himself made the best plea for segregation of prisoners of any I heard. I think he said that there were not more than one hundred prisoners in Kingston -he was speaking of Kingston particularly -who were of a violent sort, and that the others were, to use what I think was his term,
law-abiding citizens: I suppose he meant to say they did not give much trouble. One hundred out of something like-I forget at the moment what the population of the Kingston penitentiaiy is; at any rate they are a small part of the total. Superintendent Ormond gave the percentage of incorrigibles as fifteen. In another part of the same report he said that twenty per cent belonged to the bom criminal class. Nickle, Biggar and Draper in the report of 1921 said that fifteen per cent had given trouble, and not more than five percent were difficult to control. From all this I think we can conclude that only a small percentage of the prisoners are incorrigibles. Therefore it would seem a logical and sensible thing to segregate these, and try our best to save the others, not only for their own sake but for the sake of society to which they must one day be returned. Because if these men continue to be criminals they are going to cause destruction to life and property, with a great deal of suffering and misery to people outside the prison.
I feel that the government of Canada should no longer refuse to have an impartial investigation into our penal institutions. If they do, the responsibility must be entirely on the shoulders of the administration. We have done as much as we can do; newspapers and societies and a great number of people as individuals have said there should be an investigation. I believe that the public will never be satisfied until there is one, and I urge upon the government once more that it be held.
Before I resume my seat I would like to ask the Minister of Justice if it is true that Colonel Megloughlin is to be given a position in the civil service, as reported in an Ottawa paper just the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I know nothing of the report, nor of any foundation for such a rumour.
I should like to detain the committee at some length in regard to the situation spoken of by the hon. member, but as I understand His Excellency is on his way to the parliament buildings, I shall have to reserve my answer to a future occasion, in order that what I think is the desire of everyone may be complied with and the house enabled to prorogue.

The minister has
taken a most remarkable attitude.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have given my reason.

The minister has given his reason and I regard the reason as
